speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on an urgent matter.
Referring to VIA Rail Canada Inc., the Commissioner of Official Languages stated in his report that the quality of
services in French on the trains remains quite inadequate throughout the country, even on lines crossing Quebec, because VIA Rail Canada continues to give priority to the principle of seniority in the choice of routes by its staff, with the inevitable result that too frequently the trains are manned by unilingual crews. Such a situation, which is ridiculous besides being frustrating and which might be hazardous, goes against the intent of the Official Languages Act, and particularly falls short of the promise concerning French services made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) and others during the referendum campaign. Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance who will know that yesterday his deputy minister testified that the Department of Finance is taking a very hard look at a new tax on Canadian workers, called generally a tax-based incomes policy. The minister will recall that in one of his own rare pronouncements recently on economic policy on May 6, he said:
A tax-based incomes policy has not yet been devised that is both administratively feasible and fair. In particular, I have yet to see a TIP design that ultimately controls anything more than wage demands-
That was the position of the minister on May 6. First, is the government in fact looking at this new tax on Canadian workers? Second, have the minister's objections to the designs then before him been overcome, and is there a new design? Third, does the new tax his department is studying control anything more than wage demands?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is true that I mentioned a number of alternatives in that speech, I believe, before the Conference Board, including a TIP as it is called. I said that I had not seen a program which would recommend itself to me, but that the search was still going on. That is the situation as it is today; there has not been any new insight conveyed to me as to a workable and fair program.
As the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition may recall, I talked about the design of such a program and that a search for a suitable design would be continuing. That is the situation as it is now.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, perhaps the minister can give us a statement on the government's policy as to the kind of tax system which would be acceptable to it. If he does not find a design which does not have any effect other than controlling wage demands, if that is the only kind of design before him, will he reject this TIP approach?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question is hypothetical, because I cannot foresee what further study or research migh reveal. But I believe the situation is clear, it is a proposal which one ought to look at in the light of inflationary pressure. One has to be sure that it is fair and administratively feasible and has a design which would bring that about. We have not found one yet; we are still looking. I believe that is
what my deputy minister conveyed yesterday before the Senate committee.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, let me pursue for a moment this question of fairness. The minister knows that, given the rate of inflation, the real income of Canadian workers has fallen. He knows that the average Canadian worker is now earning, in real terms, more than $500 a year less than he or she was earning in 1977. These people are the principal victims of inflation in Canada. Will the minister indicate how he could justify making these people, who are now the chief victims of inflation, also the chief targets of a new tax? Particularly when the government is prepared to be as helpful as it is to companies like Petro-Canada and to individuals like Maurice Strong, how can the minister justify dumping this special tax upon people?
And to companies like Imperial.
To companies like Imperial Oil, indeed. How can he justify helping out multinationals when he proposes to add to the cost burden of the average Canadian worker?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the day ever comes when I will recommend such a program to the House of Commons, I assure my right hon. friend that I will be in a position to justify it to most sensible people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday when the deputy minister of finance was before the Senate Committee on National Finance he described the effects of high interest rates as a holocaust. I would go further and suggest that it is a holocaust in which wage earners and home owners have been the real victims. He also indicated that they would continue.
In June the minister gave an assurance in the House that the government "would not attempt to solve the economic problems of the country or the fiscal requirements of the government on the backs of the low income people of this country."
In view of the fact the minister's deputy indicated yesterday that deindexing was a real consideration at the present time and, as the Leader of the Opposition has indicated, real incomes in this country are declining, and given the fact that deindexing will tax the average wage earner and let the high income earners of the country go free, is the minister prepared to give an assurance now, in light of the uncertainties which have been created, that there will be no deindexing?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we went around this
May 28, 1981

track last year. He ought not to draw any particular conclusions from that with respect to indexation.
I should remind the hon. member and the Leader of the Opposition that when they talk about declines in real incomes in Canada, there has been a decline in productivity in Canada. It is about time hon. members opposite focus on the fact that you cannot have more by producing less. That is precisely what is happening in the country.

Madam Speaker, I want to bring a matter which is of concern to the House to the attention of the government. It has to do with the position in which we find ourselves under the Representation Act. When I was president of the privy council, I placed the appropriate reference on the order paper dealing with the representation in the House and, indeed, the question of the number of members of Parliament there ought to be in this House.
This arises because of an estimate given by the Chief Electoral Officer that, if nothing is done by Parliament and the matter is just allowed to lie, this House will expand in membership from 282 members now to a new high of 312 members after the next census. That would have an impact on cost. As the government House leader must know, the raw cost is about $170,000 per extra member, not counting support staff, buildings, housing, furniture and a host of other things. I wonder what the intention of the government is with respect to this.
If the government does nothing, then as my hon. friend knows the natural course of events will take place. The membership in the House will grow and grow, and the problem of the 1974 Parliament, which was denied then, will be passed on to a further Parliament. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the issue raised by my learned colleague is very important, and it is a fact that according to available statistics, if the new electoral boundaries were applied under the present legislation at the next federal election, there could be up to thirty additional members in this House. However, it is far from sure that these new boundaries will be in effect at the next general election because, as my colleague is aware, under the present mechanisms, which are based on Section 51 of the Canadian Constitution and the various provisions of the Electoral

May 28, 1981
Business of the House
Boundaries Act, we could wait for as long as over three years before these final boundaries are in effect.
Let me simply remind him that the June 3 census will have to be completed within a year and that following the report of the Chief Statistician of Canada, it could take more than a year and a half before the various commissions set up for each province submit their report. In addition, they are entitled to a six-month extension. Ultimately, after the reports of the various commissions have been received my learned colleague is well aware that the new boundaries can be implemented only if Parliament is dissolved more than a year later.
All of this means that, for all practical purposes, we may have to wait between two and a half and three and a half years as of today before facing the possibility of 30 additional members or implementing the new boundaries. As for the next election, nothing is certain. No one cay say definitely that, under the present provisions of the Constitution, there will surely be 30 additional members after the next election. This remains uncertain. However, 1 am not suggesting that we refuse to deal with this matter. It concerns electoral reform in general. The Speech from the Throne mentioned that a parliamentary committee will have to be set up to consider electoral reform in general. This includes proportional representation, but the general theme will be electoral reform. I feel that since this would lead ultimately to an amendment to Section 51 of the Constitution, it would be sensible and wise to wait for a few weeks before making any change that might involve amendments to the Constitution.

In dealing with Bill C-57, which is a result of the finance minister's budget, we find that a number of energy matters pertain directly to the National Energy Program and a number of tax items which are included in this legislation. The tax items in the legislation affect the farming population with respect to the sales tax exemption for equipment. Included in the legislation is a tax exemption for equipment used by school boards and universities. There are restrictions on sales tax exemptions on equipment used by fishermen. There are also tax measures pertaining to advertising flyers, a subject about which I wish to speak.
As I am sure a good many hon. members are aware, the publisher of the Edmonton Journal appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when this bill was before it to express his reservations on matters pertaining to this issue. There will be a number of newspapers adversely affected by this measure. I am sure the negative impact will be much greater on small weekly papers than it will be on large dailies. Mr. O'Callaghan, the publisher of the Edmonton Journal, expressed his views and concerns with respect to this issue when he appeared before the committee. I am hopeful that the ministers who are responsible for this legislation, and hon. members opposite, will pay heed to Mr. O'Callaghan's contribution. In my opinion he is one of Canada's finest publishers. He has spoken loudly and fought for justice and liberty for a free press and for equality for all. Regrettably, members opposite have far too often attempted to muzzle our free and democratic press.
I would like briefly to touch upon some of the energy issues which are in this legislation. Our party's critic, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), touched upon some of the issues when he spoke on Tuesday. I would like to reiterate some of the concerns expressed by him at that time since there are measures in this legislation which have proved to be the most damaging elements of the National Energy Program. The tax measures contained in this legislation will have an extremely detrimental effect on the oil and gas industry, one of the few growth industries in Canada at the present time.
I would like to cite some figures to you, Mr. Speaker. Drilling activity in Canada this year as compared with last is down by over 50 per cent. The sales potential of petroleum properties is down 70 per cent this year as compared with last. The number of drilling rigs which have left our country number some 139. These figures prove with great clarity that the National Energy Program is having a detrimental effect on self-sufficiency as far as oil is concerned. We have a number of

On behalf of our members, and for the benefit of all Canadians who are, or will, use natural gas or natural gas byproducts as a source of energy, we protest the imposition of the recently announced natural gas excise tax.
This excise tax will have particularly harsh effects on those with low or fixed incomes, unskilled wage earners, elderly pensioners, and farmers who have only limited opportunity to recover this additional cost.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in the debate on this very important bill, especially the provisions relating to petroleum. I call them the petroleum elements of the bill, and I would like to say a few words about them.
There are two petroleum elements. The first one is the 8 per cent PGRT, which is the petroleum and gas revenue tax, and it is a very important and controversial provision of this bill. It is so important that to a limited extent the negotiations with Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia on the new oil pricing agreement, which this country badly needs, are being held up just because of this particular tax. Canadians are probably a bit mystified why that would happen and what is involved. I hope to say a little bit about that in my speech.
Just to set the matter in some sort of context, we are talking about a pile of money which is being sliced up between the federal government and the provinces. We are talking about $100 billion. That is what is involved, not only the 8 per cent wellhead tax but the whole split in revenue between the provinces and the federal government. That is why there is
Excise Tax
such a crucial dispute in this country. That is the first element I want to speak to on the bill, the 8 per cent wellhead tax. We call it the wellhead tax, the tax at the wellhead. The federal government hopes to raise some revenue by this provision in the bill. The provinces are up in arms about this and I will tell the House why in a moment.
The second petroleum element of this bill is the excise tax on natural gas, and I want to say something about that. It is very important that I do so because very little has been said in the House about that particular tax. It is very important that a member of Parliament from British Columbia, as I am, say something about that tax because it has a tremendous effect on the people of the province of British Columbia. We British Columbians know that if it has an effect on us, then it has an effect on Canadians generally. I want to come back and speak about that tax, to tell Your Honour how it has an effect and what should happen to these taxes.
Let me start with the 8 per cent wellhead tax. As I have said, it is simply a means for the federal government to get more revenue and more dollars. I do not think that we on this side of the House in the New Democratic Party dispute the fact that the Government of Canada needs money to carry on. It does not spend it very well. It throws it away by spending $2 billion a year for jet planes that do not work and money for ships that do not go, and so on; but by and large, it does need money for social and economic programs and for all sorts of things which affect the average Canadian and indeed all of us.
It is typical, however, that instead of looking to the Income Tax Act, which is the normal method that the federal government uses in raising money-and I mean the main method of raising money-the federal government introduces a wellhead tax. Everyone knows we all pay income taxes, except maybe Shell or similar companies. However, most of the ordinary people in this country have to pay income taxes every year. Most of the companies in this country pay income taxes. Instead of looking to the Income Tax Act, where there is a present effective rate of 11 per cent for the oil companies, for getting more revenue by taxing these companies, the federal government has introduced a new tax, the 8 per cent wellhead tax. In my view, it is designed to hurt the very people that the federal government said it intended to help.
Let me explain why I say that. If the government had tightened up the Income Tax Act, it could have taxed the profits of the companies. The profits of oil companies and banks have been incredible in the last few years, especially those of oil companies. We have pointed that out time and time again in the House of Commons. We have pointed out that some companies have not been paying tax. In 1979 Shell paid no tax. So what has the federal government done? Instead of taking broad tax measures under the Income Tax Act, it brings in this 8 per cent tax which taxes the upstream profits of the companies.
Now, I must explain the difference between upstream and downstream. I know all fishermen would understand that, but I will try to explain it in the context of oil. "Upstream" means the place where the oil and the gas is found. I have had to

May 28, 1981
Excise Tax
learn this, Mr. Speaker. Having been a criminal lawyer and then coming into the oil and gas field, 1 have had to learn these concepts. They are not difficult and I shall try to explain them simply. The upstream is where the oil and gas is found, where the drilling is done and the gas is brought out of the ground. As I understand it, and I may be corrected, a lot of small Canadian companies are involved in drilling, exploration, servicing rigs, bringing in the water and bringing in the gas- doing all sorts of things. Profits are made in those areas when oil and gas is sold downstream.
"Downstream" is the pipelining, the refining and the marketing. The downstream is controlled by the large multinational oil companies-Imperial, Shell, Gulf and Texaco.
This particular tax, however, really hits the people upstream and not the people downstream. The government produced a petroleum monitoring report which showed that small Canadian companies reinvested the money they made when they found oil and gas and sold it. Some of the multinational oil companies like to take a profit and send it to their American shareholders or put it into solar energy or coal or some other investments.
Because of the tax on the upstream operation, small business people from Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia come to see us and say: "We are losing our business. Why are you taxing us? It is really hurting". Imperial Oil or any of the large companies have not come to us to say that they are hurting. As a matter of fact, their shares went up in value after some recent announcements by the government. The government has put the tax on in the wrong place, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday the minister said: "There is more and more exploration; look at the figures". Then he gave out-of-date figures from last year. Mr. Speaker, we saw people in the flesh-live witnesses who visited us-complain that the tax is hurting them and that they may go bankrupt. These are the little guys, not the big guys, and we on this side of the House are prepared to listen to them, even if the government is not. We are prepared to ask the government to get rid of the 8 per cent wellhead tax and change the corporate income tax to get money that way.
There is another problem, Mr. Speaker. The west is alienated. The government has a lot of difficulty dealing with the west because its power base is in the east. I was struck by the tirade delivered by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in the House yesterday when he said that the west is not suffering. The party across the way puts itself forward as the party of national unity; but it cannot be a party of national unity if it does not listen to the west. It is easy to win elections-just take Quebec and Ontario, with low-priced oil in Ontario, and pretend that its interests are being looked after-although in the long run they are not- keep the solid base because of the many members from Quebec, and the result is permanent government in Canada.
There is a real problem in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. In its own way, it is having the same kind of revolution as that
which happened in Quebec in the sixties. I suspect many members opposite, including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, came to this House as the result of Pearsonian Liberalism or as a result of feeling that there was a role for the federal government to play in co-operative federalism with the provinces.
This tax hurts co-operative federalism, Mr. Speaker, and I urge the government to consider it again. I do not make the argument that the provinces cannot afford it; I make the argument for the little guy. I am in favour of provincial revenues, but I believe there should be a better way of dealing with the provinces in respect of this 8 per cent tax.
It does not make sense to hurt the little guy upstream and forget about the big guys downstream, Mr. Speaker. That is where the tax should be applied. The same amount of money could be raised, the western provinces would be satisfied and the small businessmen in Alberta, B.C. and Saskatchewan would be satisfied, as would the principles of co-operative federalism.
I now want to deal with the subject of gas, Mr. Speaker. There is a problem with federalism when it comes to gas. This party is not opposed to the principle of a tax on gas but this is not a good time for it. My constituents want to know why there is a tax on natural gas which is produced by the western provinces-mainly British Columbia-when there is no tax on Quebec electricity or on Ontario gold and nickel or hydro. I find it difficult to answer them. I could say it is a source of revenue, but, Mr. Speaker, this is a bad time to levy that tax. At the time the Petroleum Administration Act was imposed unilaterally by the federal government, we as a party urged the minister to consider that tax again.
There is another reason why the tax should not be imposed, Mr. Speaker. There is a glut of gas in the United States at the moment. In 1979, the Clark government raised the gas export price and, as a result, the United States has not been buying British Columbia gas. Now, at the same time as the price of gas increases as a result of this tax, exports are decreasing.
The government has not allowed any change in the price of export gas. The result, as the economists would say, is that they have "used up the space". A tax has been imposed but we cannot get any more money for our exports, so who is to pay the tax? It is the people of British Columbia who will bear the burden.
It comes at an awkward time for British Columbia because the provincial government has been subsidizing the price of natural gas to the tune of $100 million per year. As a result, last year 40 per cent less gas was sold than the year before. Instead of the subsidy coming out of the sale of gas exports, it really comes out of British Columbia's general revenue. I am just trying to put the facts before the government because it does not have any members from British Columbia in its ranks and may not know this!
British Columbia had planned to raise the price of gas to consumers this year. At the moment, 1,000 cubic feet of gas costs $1.20. As a result of this bill we are debating today, a
May 28, 1981

41-cent tax will be imposed by July 1 and the province will likely impose another tax of about 60 cents. The price of gas for British Columbia consumers will be doubled.
It does not make much sense, Mr. Speaker, for the government to have a policy of switching off expensive imported oil for cheap Canadian natural gas, when the price of the Canadian natural gas is doubled. The actual impact in British Columbia will not be for people to switch from oil to gas, as the National Energy Program proposes; in fact, it will scare British Columbia away from switching to gas. They see a discriminatory tax. They see the price doubling. British Columbians will not convert to gas.
I am informed that this morning the Saskatchewan government filed a suit in its court of appeal against the federal government, challenging the federal government's ability to tax provincial Crown corporations. This lawsuit is of particular interest to the people of British Columbia. We market our gas through a Crown corporation called the BCPC, which is the British Columbia Petroleum Corporation. We used to have a socialist government in British Columbia, so we do not let the downstreamers take all the profit. We take the profit and distribute it among the people. BCPC buys gas from the producers and either sells it to the people or it is exported. BC Hydro is involved.
This lawsuit filed this morning by the Saskatchewan government will be watched very carefully by British Columbians. It will deal with the principle of whether a provincial Crown corporation can be taxed. It is not the lawsuit that I am pointing out but the fact that the government could have avoided the danger of lawsuits and disputes between itself and the provinces. We do not need that. These things should be settled in a different way, not through the courts. They should be settled through negotiation. That is what co-operative federalism is all about.
This tax is a divisive tax. By devious methods, the minister of energy is trying to raise money to deal with a particular problem. What he should do is negotiate up front with the provinces instead of levying these new taxes.
In summary, the taxes are against the principles of co-operative federalism. They are discriminatory against one region of the country. They hurt the little guy. They do very little to take additional revenues from the big companies. Instead, Canadians will end up with higher prices and higher costs at times when we really cannot afford to pay them. These costs will fall on the consumer, not on the big producers and markets.
While we on this side of the House are in favour of the principle of taxation and while we are in favour of the federal government being active and having a major role to play in this country, we must tell our friends across the way on the government side that this is not the way to do it and to delete these clauses from the bill.

Again, a slap on the wrist should be given to the provincial treasurer of Ontario. I guess he learned the dirty trick from the Minister of Finance.
I find it difficult to accept that, because this government is not able to control inflation, it will use inflation to index taxes. In other words, the higher inflation goes, the more money that will roll into the government's coffers. I do not think anyone would disagree with me about that. Even members on the government side of the House should be shaking their heads and agreeing with me.
This measure will allow the government to benefit from the inflation it has created. I hear the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) interjecting. The government is benefiting because of inflation, yet we hear the government telling us that it will do its very best to control inflation. To do that very thing, the government is keeping interest rates high. But at the same time this government is driving a good many businessmen to the brink of bankruptcy. Some will declare bankruptcy. I know a great many small businesses in my riding that are feeling the pinch. I am quite sure the Minister of State for Finance knows that as well. Possibly there are some small businesses going bankrupt in his own area because of high interest rates. This is an absolute disgrace. Reasonably successful businessmen who have been established for a long while are going to the bank to borrow money to meet operating costs or to purchase inventory during their busy seasons and are having to pay 21 per cent interest.
I also wish to express my concern and the concern of many others at what appears to be evident departures from the normal calculation of excise taxes. As the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, excise tax has been commonly known as the manufacturers' sales tax. This tax was imposed upon the price at which a manufacturer would sell his or her products. The bill before this House seems to be shifting the excise tax away from the manufacturer to the wholesaler and distributor. This will ultimately lead to a greater Financial burden on the consumer and will generate extra funds for the government.
I am quite sure that many other members of Parliament as well as 1 have received letters criticizing the government for this change in policy. I certainly hope the government will rethink this. This government does not need to print extra money; it simply digs a little deeper into the pockets of tax-paying Canadians. By this bill it looks as though the government wants to dig a little deeper into the pockets of certain segments of the nation which can ill afford to support this government greed.
I want to discuss the impact of the clause of this bill dealing with excise taxes on advertising and advertising supplements in small community newspapers. There are many small weekly papers in my riding, as in many ridings across the country, which offer the community a valuable service by providing news, information and entertainment. These newspapers, which do not have the financial resources of large corporations or the revenue resources of those in larger centres, are very dependent upon the advertising they obtain. The imposition of the excise tax as outlined in this bill would place the operations of these important papers in jeopardy. I hope the government will reconsider this matter, recognize the value and contribution of community newspapers and exempt those serving certain sized populations from this change in the taxing method.
I want also to express my opposition to that part of the bill which deals with the production of gasohol. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) mentioned when speaking on this issue, gasohol is legal and its use encouraged in over 30 of the world's nations. Why Canada, or at least the present Canadian government, should take a different stand is certainly beyond me.
Other governments have realized the potential of gasohol in certain circumstances and have supported its use. This government, however, seems to be determined to ignore it or, at the very least, will penalize Canadians who want to use gasohol as a fuel alternative. The bill before us reflects the government's attitude. It does not use the word "gasohol"; it refers to the product as "denatured spirits." This just means alcohol that is rendered unfit to drink.
The government seems less worried about the advantages of Canadians using gasohol for fuel as it is about the possibility that some Canadians will erect stills to produce alcohol for human consumption. Under this bill the government will grant a special temporary licence for the manufacture of denatured spirits which are to be used solely in experimentation and development of a fuel. Surely the government realizes that such experimentation and development has been going on for centuries now, probably for a few thousand years, and the process is fairly straightforward. There are experimental processes taking place in respect of alternative approaches to manufacture, both in the conversion and separation stages, but the simple distillation process is relatively unchanged.
Why in the world would the government want to limit licences for experimentation only when many Canadians have

gone beyond that stage and are into production, illegally now,
I must point out? In my own riding we had an individual who had gone beyond the experimental stage and was in fact using gasohol to power his own vehicle. He was not only successful in producing the product, he was producing it cheaply. to force people to buy, even when it is for their own use. The premiums on surety bonds and fidelity bonds are quite high now. In many cases it is quite difficult to have insurance placed. Mr. Speaker, normally when I rise to speak in this House I do so with considerable pleasure and enthusiasm. However, with respect to Bill C-57 I must confess it is extremely difficult to be very enthusiastic. This is a tax bill, and no one likes a bill which purports to take money from Canadian businessmen or from individual Canadian taxpayers, even though I think we all realize that from time to time such bills are necessary.
However, this bill is particularly distasteful. As tax bills go-and they go a long way-I might say that this bill is an absolute horror. More than that, it is a disgrace because it does nothing more than reflect this governement's complete mismanagement of the economy, and it underlines this government's desperation for money.
I intend to speak generally about this bill in the short time I have available to me. However, in my remarks I will highlight two areas of the bill which I believe are particularly wrong and ill-advised at this time.
The first area to which I will refer is the government's attempt to index taxation to inflation, as it purports to do with its treatment of the tax on alcoholic beverages. The second area of my concern is the 8 per cent tax on petroleum and gas products. Ever since about 1973 when this government started deficit financing, it has continually spent more than it has received. Since 1973 deficit financing has become a way of life, as the Liberals have acted out their basic philosophy of government, which is that any problem in this country can be solved if they, the Liberals, can only throw enough money and enough bureaucrats at it. My oh my, the Liberals have certainly thrown enough money and hired enough bureaucrats over the past number of years, and they have done so to the point that today we have a yearly deficit of some $14 billion and a total deficit of $107 billion. I do not understand the magnitude of those figures. I cannot even imagine it.
With respect to the civil service, we must certainly be the overgoverned country of the western world. It is not surprising that, as a result of all this activity by the Liberal party, the country is bankrupt. The government is short of money and desperate for cash. There is a dire necessity for government restraint, but herein lies the difficulty. This government, and its bureaucrats who created the mess, are simply not capable of solving the problem. They simply cannot find the strength of will or the determination to cut back on government expenditures or to show any kind of restraint. It is like asking a firebug to put out the fire: he is emotionally incapable of doing so. When we ask this government to cut funding, it cannot do so.
What is the Liberal solution to this problem? The Liberal solution is to beg, borrow, wring, squeeze and, yes, even steal
money from the Canadian public. This government and its bureaucrats have discovered three ways to get money. I think the scheme is mostly that of the bureaucrats because I do not believe the occupants of the Liberal front bench are bright enough to conceive of the Machiavellian measures which are now being set in place. The occupants of the Liberal front bench are tired. They are the ones who started the mess. This is the worst front bench any Canadian government has displayed or Canadians have had to contend with as an excuse for government in a long time.
The only claim to fame of the occupants of the back bench is their knee-jerk response and their haste to say "Yes, Sir" to each and every crazy scheme proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). One must wonder what they do in caucus other than discuss the length of the forthcoming recess, the terms of their pensions or even the size of their salaries. So the measures before us must come from the bureaucrats. In order to save their jobs and keep their ridiculously high salaries, it is they who come up with the grand design, and the Liberal government is carrying out the plan to squeeze more cash out of the Canadian public.
The grand design is threefold. The first method is inflation. This is an old standby used by many governments in many countries. There is always eventually the same result of runaway inflation and eventual collapse. It is a fairly useful gimmick. It fools the public for a short time and allows the government to finance its huge deficits. If you have an annual deficit of $14 billion and a total deficit of $107 billion, how do you pay this money back? The answer, of course, is to devalue the currency and soon we find it is easier to pay back good dollars with a cheap 75-cent dollar, a cheap 50-cent dollar, or an even cheaper 25-cent dollar, wherever and how far the public will let it go. This is the Liberal plan.
What are the mechanics of this plan? There are several. First of all, print money. The Liberal government over the years has constantly increased the money supply. Secondly, the government must make certain that money policy includes high interest rates, and they have done this. Who can deny that high interest rates are inflationary, particularly when they are not accompanied by fiscal policies and government restraint? It takes no genius to see, and only a Liberal would fail to see, that an increase in the bank rate increases the cost of production of all goods and services. The small and indeed even the large businessman paying 20 per cent to finance his inventory has to charge a good deal more than if he is only financing at 10 per cent.
If this government is serious about controlling inflation, where is the tight money policy that should be established? We do not have one; you can borrow all the money you want at high interest rates. If you are prepared to pay the 20 to 21 per cent mentioned by previous speakers, the money supply and the debt continues to grow.
Now, how else does this government encourage inflation? One method it is using is to cause the Canadian dollar to drop
May 28, 1981

in value vis-a-vis other currencies, particularly the U.S. dollar. Consequently all the things we buy from outside Canada- fresh fruit, vegetables, capital goods, vacations-indeed everything, costs more and thus further fuels inflation. I suggest that the Liberal government achieved this fall in value of the dollar by keeping Canadian productivity at an unreasonable and uncompetitive level, by allowing investment in research and development to fall to disgraceful levels, and by failing to provide an industrial strategy for Canada in the 1970s and the 1980s, particularly for Ontario and Quebec. It is just another part of the horror story of the Liberal regime and it is extremely difficult to believe it was all accidental or the result of stupidity.
How else does the government cause inflation? Well, this government has some new and different kicks. Firstly, it spent over $1.3 billion to purchase a non-productive retail oil company which will not result in one extra barrel of oil in Canada or one extra job for Canadians. It then proceeds to charge this huge expense directly to the poor auto driver by gouging him at the gas pumps. And that, I suggest, is deliberately inflationary.
What else does this Liberal government do? It pays to foreign countries over $3.2 billion annually to buy high-priced oil because of a stupid political position, and that money is taken directly out of the pockets of Canadians to enhance the wealth of other countries. And that, Mr. Speaker, I suggest is inflationary.
Finally, as proof positive that this government wants to encourage inflation and that it is part of its package of fiscal tools to pay for the huge deficit, we have this bill before us which proposes to index tax increases to inflation. By this act, the government proposes to introduce automatic tax increases on alcoholic beverages so that in the future taxes are increased automatically whether or not the government needs the money. By this insidious device taxes will increase without reference to Parliament, without discussion or explanation whatsoever to the Canadian public as to the need for the increase.
In the peculiar way this government has imposed this tax on the industry, the result has been to discourage the consumption of beverages of low alcoholic content, beer and wine, and encourage the consumption of hard liquor. Surely a strange thing for a government to do and reason enough to change this legislation.
The terrible aspect of this tax is the fact that it is tied to inflation and that the government automatically receives more taxes without reference to Parliament. It will be taxing people on inflation; thus it has a vested interest in seeing that inflation continues. By indexing this tax, the government is formally giving notice that it endorses and encourages inflation as a part of its fiscal policy. No wonder Canadians across this country have lost confidence; no wonder that, in spite of the higher interest rates, Canadians are going on a buying binge and consequently rendering ineffective the high interest rate policy.
What is step number two in the grand design to obtain cash to pay its debts? Well, we all know by now it is the huge power
Excise Tax
and money grab on provincial resources. Not all provinces, however. The Liberals may be stupid economically but they are politically rather wise and identify their power with a majority in Quebec and strong support in Ontario, so these provinces generally will escape the resource grab. However, God or the Supreme Court will have to intervene to stop the resource grab in the rest of the country. The Liberals are taking the offshore resources of the Atlantic provinces. They are stealing the aboriginal rights of the Indian, Inuit and Metis and the lands of other people of northern Canada. Finally, and most aggressively of all, they are determined to rob the resource wealth of western Canada. The resource wealth of the west is the key to the Liberal program to obtain more cash and feed the insatiable bureaucrats' appetite for more and more spending.
A keystone in the government program to achieve this is the introduction in this bill of a petroleum and gas revenue tax. The act proposes to tax these products at the rate of 8 per cent of all revenues from production of oil and gas. It is not surprising that this tax has met strong opposition from the provinces since they charge, and rightfully so, that it makes nonsense of their constitutional right to own and exploit their natural resources.
In its method of application the tax is more in the nature of a royalty and in fact has been held as unconstitutional by the Alberta appeal court. Aside from that, the practical effect on the economy and well-being of the petroleum industry has been and is disastrous. Other speakers have described the results: 139 rigs have left the country; drilling activity has been reduced; sales of petroleum properties have declined.
The slowdown in the oil industry affects everyone. Out of every dollar the oil industry spends, 42 cents is spent in Ontario, 13 cents in Quebec, 29 cents in Alberta and 16 cents in other provinces. For every job created in Alberta in the oil industry, two are created in the rest of Canada. The loss of jobs and economic activity in Canada is almost beyond calculation.
And so goes the horror story. One can only stand back in amazement at a government which in a grand manner proclaims a national energy policy, one calling for oil self-sufficiency by 1990, and then proceeds to impose punitive taxation and ridiculous regulation sufficient to wreck the industry and ruin the economy in less than a year.
What are we told now? We are now told that the advisers of the Prime Minister are telling cabinet that the big shock in the eighties will be that there will be no jobs in central Canada for young people; there will be no jobs in Quebec or in Ontario. In fact, there will be no jobs for any of these people in the early eighties. What will they do? The advisers of the Prime Minister are telling us that some 500,000 young people-perhaps even a million-from Quebec and Ontario will have to move west to find jobs, work, security and employment.
The Trudeau government has failed these young people by failing to provide an industrial strategy or design for the

May 28, 1981

industrial provinces of central Canada. The Trudeau government has failed to maintain an adequate or competitive industrial climate by not providing or encouraging sufficient research and development. The young people of Quebec and Ontario are now reaping the rewards of this Liberal government's stupid and ineffective economic policies. But the wonder of wonders is: Do these young people know that when they head west to the promised land, Trudeau and Lalonde will have been there before them?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) for getting me an audience. I want to make a few comments in this debate this afternoon. I will not speak long, but I want to sound a warning to my colleagues from other parts of Canada about the effects the National Energy Program is having in western
Canada and about the perceptions of western Canadians of our country, perceptions of deep concern to me.
Specifically I want to speak about the 8 per cent tax on gas and oil production in the bill before us today. This tax points out the policy of the government across the way. It is a policy more of confrontive federalism than co-operative federalism. It is a policy which is arousing the ire and concern of more and more reasonable people in the west. In fact, this morning the government of Saskatchewan took a challenge to the Court of Appeal of Saskatchewan on the 8 per cent tax on the production of gas and oil. I predict this challenge will end up in the Supreme Court of Canada, either appealed by the Saskatchewan government or by the federal government, depending upon whether or not Saskatchewan wins its case in its own court. The main reason they are challenging the legislation is that, for the first time in our history, the federal government is taxing provincial Crown corporations. I suggest that move is wrong.
In fact, I believe the entire 8 per cent tax is wrong. It is wrong for the following six reasons. It is wrong because it is a regressive tax. The 8 per cent tax hits the large companies like Imperial Oil as hard as it hits the small companies in Saskatchewan and Alberta. It does not differentiate between the rich and the poor oil companies in the country. For those reasons I believe it is wrong.
Also it is wrong because, as I said, it taxes Crown corporations. Who would have dreamt a few years ago that the Government of Canada would impose in a budget a tax on provincial Crown corporations? What kind of dangerous precedent or what kind of constitutional war could the country become involved in if the Government of Canada gets its way in imposing unilaterally, without notice or negotiation, a tax on the Crown corporations of the country which are owned by the people through their provincial governments? There is a danger that the provincial governments will retaliate and impose a tax on federal Crown corporations such as Petro-Canada, Air Canada and CNR. What kind of a war will there be between the federal government and the provinces if this type of nonsense goes on?
Third, it has been previously documented in the House by my party that a number of people are losing their jobs because of the national energy policy and the 8 per cent tax. I am thinking of southern Saskatchewan, western Saskatchewan and the area of my colleague, the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish), where people are losing their jobs because of the fact that the national energy policy is imposing a tax which is driving rigs out of the country.
Fourth, I believe that when the government imposes the 8 per cent tax, not only the companies pay. Eventually it will pass the tax on to the consumer, and the consumer will be paying at least 8 per cent more for petroleum products, for gas to heat their homes, for gasoline to drive their cars, for farm fuel and the like.
Fifth, it is also wrong because it represents what I believe is an illegitimate revenue grab by the federal government in a
May 28, 1981

field of provincial concern. This aggravates or increases some of the grievances of the provinces about confederation.
Finally, I believe the 8 per cent tax is wrong because it discriminates against western provinces. It is a tax on gas and oil. Therefore, it is a tax on Alberta and Saskatchewan primarily, but also, to a lesser degree, on the province of British Columbia. If we are to have a special tax on the production of gas and oil in those two provinces, what about a special tax on the production of mineral resources such as nickel, copper, lead and zinc which come from other parts of Canada? What about some equity in the federal system?
I make an appeal today especially to Liberal party members sitting across from me to try to make them understand that the feeling of grievance and discontent in western Canada is strong and growing.
I do not stand here today to try to sound an alarm, but I do want to try to warn hon. members across the way that there are problems in the west and that policies such as these are responsible for making more and more western Canadians alienated from the very country in which they live. It is not just this confrontive federalism, this federalism of confrontation, this fight between governments-between Alberta and Ottawa, Saskatchewan and Ottawa or British Columbia and Ottawa; it is now a fight between the people of the country.
The ordinary people in my part of Canada are becoming more and more concerned about the role they are playing in confederation. I refer to The Globe and Mail of a week ago today, May 21. On the front page there is an article which I think all members should study. The headline reads "Alienation in West on rise, poll shows." It is an article concerning a public opinion poll commissioned by the Canada West Foundation, a very well known and highly respected group in western Canada which is partially funded by the four provincial governments. A poll was taken by this organization to find out how western Canadians felt about our country and to determine what kind of perceptions we have about Canada and its future. It followed a poll which was taken by this same group last October, right after the announcement of the constitutional resolution and the National Energy Program. The poll showed in almost all instances that alienation in the west is increasing.
The following statement was put to western Canadians:
Western Canadians get so few benefits from being part of Canada that they might as well go it on their own.
Some 36 per cent of westerners agreed with that statement; 36 per cent of our people said: "We get so few benefits we might as well consider going it on our own." Last October, 28 percent agreed with that statement and now 36 per cent do so.
That kind of statistic terrifies me. I think it should also terrify the government and should motivate it in the name of Canada and in the name of unity to have all of us stick together in one state, to find out why western Canadians feel that they are discriminated against. I think the government knows we want to stay in Canada; that is what the west wants.
Excise Tax
All over the west there are many people who are loyal to our country, who fought in two great wars under the flag of this country and who want to have this country stay together.
In the same poll people were asked bluntly whether or not they wanted to separate. Some 88 per cent of those polled said: "No, we want to stay in Canada." Last October 90 per cent of those polled replied in that way. On the other hand, there is a small minority of people who want to set up a separate state. Some 7 per cent of those polled said: "Let us have a separate country". Some 3 per cent said; "Let us join the United States." And 53 per cent of the people polled said that they have more in common in their hearts with the United States than they have with the people of central and eastern Canada.
So it is my purpose today to sound a warning to this House that, if we do not start to take some of the grievances in the west seriously, there may be a movement in western Canada which will be very hard to stop, which may start to snowball.
In many ways the atmosphere found in the west today is similar to that found in Quebec 20 years ago when we saw the increasing alienation of the Quebecois to the rest of the country. Some people pooh-poohed this and said: "They are just a bunch of fanatics; they will never succeed. If we do not take them seriously and if we continue on with the status quo, or perhaps tinker here and there and make just a few reforms, then separatism in Quebec will be absolutely dead."
In the province of Quebec last year there was a referendum in which 40 per cent of the people voted yes to a question which, in essence, would have constituted a signal leading Quebecers toward an independent state. There is a great difference between the motivation for independence in Quebec and the motivation in Quebec for a different arrangement in this country than there is in western Canada. But there are also many similarities. There are similarities in the way that people feel about the country, both in the west and in Quebec. People feel that we are not equal partners or equal participants with the other parts of the country. If we do not address these problems and if impositions are made on western Canada without consultation or representation from the west, then there might be an independence movement which, once it got going, would be like a snowball or a prairie fire-very difficult to stop.
Members opposite should take my plea seriously and eliminate the 8 per cent tax, or at least change it so that it is not a discriminatory tax against the people of western Canada. I feel that very strongly, Mr. Speaker. I feel very strongly that this 8 per cent tax is not something in isolation but is part of an over-all plan by the federal government to reduce its deficit by reorganizing many of the institutions and programs which we have in our country today. It is a move away from co-operative federalism. In that kind of federalism you sit down and come up with a compromise and consensus between the provinces and the centre. What we see is a move toward confrontative federalism where impositions are placed on the regions.
We have seen that the constitutional resolution takes powers away from the provinces and gives them to the courts. This was done against the wishes of the four provinces in the west
