BRITISH COLUMBIA HYDRO-JOINT FUNDING AND PROPOSED DAMS
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House before January 31, 1981, copies of all correspondence, telegrams or other documents exchanged between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and British Columbia Hydro relating to joint funding and proposed dams in British Columbia including the names of the 20 salmon streams slated for damming.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on my motion for the production of papers. Hon. members of the House will recall that on November 20, 1980 I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) a question related to a document I had received from his department. That document was entitled the "Western Vision Blueprint", and talked about the possibility of the federal government and B.C. Hydro damming a number of rivers in British Columbia. Members will remember the indignant response the minister made, when trying to answer the question. The minister said that his officials had briefed me on the document when, in fact, they had called to plead with me not to release it.
The minister then went on to say that the issue would panic people in British Columbia. He said that outside the House, of course, because he was not able to respond adequately to me during the House of Commons question period.
I asked the minister questions about this so-called "blueprint" because of the concern I have over the possibility of this minister allowing rivers in British Columbia to be dammed without due concern for the fisheries resource. Despite the fact that the report says, and I quote:
That B.C. Hydro is looking for ways in which to meet peak power demands- many of these projects could have very attractive benefit cost ratios-there is an opportunity through joint development for both parties to meet their goals. We know B.C. Hydro is interested; we also know there are perhaps 20 or more salmon streams that would lend themselves to this approach.
That is taken from the document I received. It was prepared by Department of Fisheries and Oceans personnel, and I think it is important for hon. members of this House to have the names of those rivers and to know just exactly what this joint approach to hydro development in British Columbia involves.
The minister has refused to say which 20 rivers are going to be dammed and also by his silence has indicated he is not willing to tell the House what discussions have gone on between his department and B.C. Hydro.
It is therefore clear to me that when the government issues a report that says there are 20 rivers to be dammed, that identifies a five-year funding program and a financial flow, and all of this is set out in a very clear, technical way in the report, someone in the department of the Minister of Fisheries
Hydro Development
and Oceans has been looking at this very seriously. How does the government know that B.C. Hydro is interested? What kinds of correspondence and discussions have been held between the two? Or are we to assume that the minister and Bob Bonner have been quietly communicating telepathically?
In light of the minister's refusal to provide the House with any additional information whatsoever, I placed my motion on the Order Paper to have copies of correspondence, telegrams, or other documents tabled in the House by January 31, 1981. On December 17, 1980, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette) asked me to withdraw the motion. 1 asked to have the motion transferred for debate. We are going to have the debate today and at a future date.
After some research, I am glad to be able to speak in a more technical manner on this issue today. Perhaps I should not say "glad" because some of the information I have come across leads me to seriously question the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council's statement that no documents exist regarding the issue. Even more importantly is the information that indicates that this government is willing to sell out the fisheries resource in British Columbia, just as they have done on the Kemano issue, Amax, the Fraser River and others.
I am sure Your Honour will recall that on several dozen occasions I raised the question of Amax, a mining company which is being allowed to dump 12,000 tons of toxic effluent a day into Alice Arm. The statements I made in this House were refuted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), and need I go on? My statements have now been proven to be correct. Amax was, in fact, closed this morning because the tailings were resurfacing.
It comes right down to the crunch. If a document is prepared by fisheries and oceans, has a flow chart, gives a specific number of rivers, and names the actual figures which are under discussion for these joint developments, I think that when an hon. member gives notice of motion for the production of papers that he knows exist, or at least has some reason to suppose they exist, there is a responsibility on the government side to provide them as sheer information. We do not have a freedom of information act. It is important to hon. members, particularly those from British Columbia, regarding this issue that we at least be provided with background information, so that we can provide our communities and, in fact, our own members of the legislative assembly in British Columbia with that information and know what is going on and have some sort of a rational planning of hydroelectric development in a province which has had a tragic history of inappropriate dam development.
The truth of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that at least one document does exist about this government's plan to dam rivers in British Columbia. In July, 1978 Crippen Consultants of Vancouver, B.C., submitted an unsolicited proposal to the

May 28, 1981
Hydro Development
Department of Supply and Services to do a study of possible hydro projects in B.C. In February, 1979, the Department of Supply and Services issued a contract to the same company. The project was to "estimate the potential for micro hydro development in remote communities in British Columbia". After much work I have been able to obtain only volume one of the two-volume report.
Let me make it clear at this point that micro hydro technology and small hydroelectric technology I am certainly very much in support of. Various European countries have come up with very innovative ways of producing hydroelectricity by small, torpedo-shaped hydraulic generation where they anchor it in the bottom of the river. The river continues to flow. The fish can go up and down and canoeists can use the river. Aesthetically it is not unpleasing. The natural flow of that fresh water into the marine environment allows the biological environment in the estuary to continue unimpeded and to maintain natural fish populations.
The report by Crippen Consultants identifies, in what they call the north coast region, 24 possible locations for micro hydro potential. In the other regions mentioned there are some 80 possible sites. A little bit of a quick calculation allows us to realize that not all streams and rivers in British Columbia have salmon. However, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in his own document, has identified possible dams on 20 salmon rivers in British Columbia which, I think, is the real key and requirement for the production of these documents.
A quick review of the report does not indicate any concerns whatsoever over the fisheries resource. It does not discuss public hearings before any of these projects would get under way. In fact, the report has a nine-page section that lists "undeveloped hydroelectric sites" in British Columbia. This section of the report talks about creeks, and even mentions such rivers in my riding as the Nass and Skeena Rivers which have been unimpeded since time immemorial.
Is the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans aware of this study, I wonder? Is the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council aware of it? Are they aware of their responsibilities in relation to the production of these documents?
In their desire to put their blinders on when looking at my motion for the production of papers, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans closed their collective eyes to some of what the other government departments were doing. The members of this House know that I am interested in developing energy resources in this country. I am also completely aware of the possibilities of developing what are referred to in the Crippen report as low head power dams, something that I think many rural areas will look into in the near future. However, I and other members of this House, including, I hope, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, know how vitally important it is to protect the fisheries habitat. The report I have uncovered and the lack of concern the minister demonstrates tell me that we have to explain this issue to him time and time again.
There is more about reports, Mr. Speaker. The Stikine River in northern British Columbia is a beautiful river that flows from the northern reaches of my riding through some of the most incredible scenery in the province of British Columbia. The Grand Canyon of the Stikine is a sight to behold. As a matter of fact, I was up there last year with the previous Premier of British Columbia, Dave Barrett. We flew through to look not only at the fisheries in and below the canyon but at one of the last large goat populations in northern British Columbia.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans chairs an interdepartmental task force that is studying the effects a proposed dam on the Stikine might have. In a letter dated November 18, 1980 to the Sierra Club in Vancouver, the Minister of the Environment wrote that the task force "has been established to provide advice to B.C. Hydro and Power Authority on study requirements and to review study progress and completed impact assessment reports".
I am aware that correspondence has been communicated from Fisheries and Oceans personnel in relation to the Stikine dam. It is an issue of international significance. I had the opportunity a few days ago to discuss the matter with Senator Ted Stevens from Alaska, who also has expressed alarm at the lack of public and international participation in relation to the fisheries resource on this particular hydroelectric proposal. The studies are being done under the auspices of British Columbia Hydro. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is involved. It is a salmon river and in my view it is one of the 20 dams referred to in the Western Visions Blueprint as one of the rivers considered for joint development by B.C. Hydro and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
It is crucially important in a riding such as mine, in communities like Telegraph Creek where the Talt and native people make their home, that a member of Parliament be able to provide information on proposals for the damming of a river that has enormous and important salmon runs which provide the ongoing and traditional diet of the people and is part of their culture. For the Department of Fisheries and Oceans not to provide the documents relating to the Stikine requested through a notice of motion for the tabling of documents is, in my view, a very rash act that hits at the core of democracy.
Is the Stikine one of the proposed 20 rivers that the Western Vision Blueprint talks about? Why was some of that advice that the Minister of the Environment talks about not tabled in response to my motion? On April 9, 1981 in response to a letter I wrote to the minister about British Columbia Hydro plans for damming rivers in B.C., the minister replied:
I am not prepared to provide you with correspondence between Environment Canada and other federal departments regarding British Columbia Hydro plans for river developments in British Columbia-
The minister has told me in a letter which is just more than a month old, that correspondence does exist between his department and other departments but that he is not prepared to release it. In this House we have notices of motion and there are procedures fundamental to the parliamentary system, but
May 28, 1981

because we do not have a freedom of information act, members of the opposition are not privy to a great deal of ministerial documents prepared by civil servants. In my view, if those studies are to have an impact in some area of the country, they should be provided to the opposition. If they are particularly sensitive or refer to national security, members of the opposition could be told that such is the case, but at least they could become informed about what is going on between various levels of government and various departments.
What is so secret about these plans that the minister will not release them? Perhaps the Minister of the Environment should tell the House if any of his officials had anything to do with writing the Western Visions Blueprint.
In a letter written to me by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on February 3, 1981, he says:
Any proposals by B.C. Hydro have always been and will continue to be presented to my department for technical review in accordance with the habitat protection provisions of the Fisheries Act.
This is precisely my point, Mr. Speaker. The minister of fisheries is speaking about precisely the documents I was attempting to obtain which were referred to in a document prepared by his department. He wrote to me after the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council asked me to withdraw my motion, saying that there were no documents. We now have confirmation from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and from correspondence with the Minister of the Environment that the documents do exist, but apparently the government does not intend to comply with an order of this House. This method has traditionally provided not only members of the opposition but in some cases members of the government with valuable and vital information which enables them to represent their constituents effectively.
I should like to refer again to the Western Visions Blueprint document. In the second part, on page 2 under the heading "Department of Fisheries and Oceans-Western Visions Blueprint-Financial Flow", item 4, "Hydro planning and pilot projects", shows $1 million for year one; $3.5 million for year two; $10.5 million for year three; $11 million for year four and $11 million for year five. In the remarks column there appears, "Assumes joint funding with B.C. Hydro .. .". This chart shows the expenditure of tens of millions of dollars jointly between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and B.C. Hydro. There are dams in my riding as I think there are in the ridings of many members from British Columbia, and I think we should have access to the information referred to in the document.
Item 7 of the document shows "Reservoir planning and pilot projects". In the first year it shows $1 million; in the second year $3 million; third year $3 million; fourth year $4 million and fifth year $4 million. The remark is, "Joint ventures with other agencies."
As if that were not enough, Mr. Speaker, under the heading "The Road to 1995" there appears the following in the text:
-the federal government could, by 1995, transform the B.C. coast, for example, or recast the script for the as yet unwritten history of those people dependent of fresh water fisheries.
Hydro Development
The people of British Columbia are not interested in the federal government alone transforming the B.C. coast, the lifestyles and traditional industries of the people who are dependent upon the fresh water fishery, without having direct involvement in and access to the information being developed. The text of the document goes on as follows:
The federal government frequently gets a negative image because ... it so frequently comes into conflict with agriculture, forestry, mining, hydro... Fisheries, and by extension the federal government, is too often seen by provincial administrations as a negative influence on other economic development. It is time for new approaches. Multiple resource management with a twist.
I am not sure who wrote the script for "The Road to 1995" but it may encourage members in their collective desire to get access to these documents.
It is interesting to note that the minister is not in the House today. I recognize that he has duties in other areas of Canada, but surely British Columbians have a right to access to planning documents that affect the rivers there.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say how important this debate is. Early next month there will be a meeting in Juneau, Alaska, where officials of the federal government, the provincial government, B.C. Hydro and Alaska state officials will meet to discuss the implications of the proposed damming of the Stikine River. I might point out that other rivers are also under consideration. Perhaps the documents that the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans have referred to in writing to me after the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council said there were none will now be released.
I believe the intent of my motion is abundantly clear: the government was to turn over documents related to the so-called Western Visions Blueprint. They say they do not exist. I believe the information I have provided to the House today shows that there are related documents, and that by its secrecy the government has shown that there probably are others.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully urge the minister and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council to go back to their offices today and ask the officials who were preparing the blueprint for their documents and to table the information in the House. To do so will respect the rules of this Parliament and will give the people of British Columbia the truth about what the government is planning to do about dams in British Columbia which may well impact on the salmon resource and other resources.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Henderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA HYDRO-JOINT FUNDING AND PROPOSED DAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems obvious that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has some kind of a bee in his bonnet over hydro dams in British Columbia and that his fertile imagination has dreamed up all kinds of sinister and clandestine deals between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and B.C. Hydro.
The hon. member has received written and verbal replies to his questions on this subject, but apparently he still needs to be

May 28, 1981
Hydro Development
convinced that the federal government is not selling out B.C.'s salmon resources to B.C. Hydro.
Let us look at the facts without all the wild speculation and allegations. The first point to be made is that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans adheres to a long-standing policy to work positively at the watershed level with other water users when it can be demonstrated that fisheries goals can be accommodated. The department's main responsibility is, of course, to protect and, wherever possible, enhance the fish stocks. Where this can be achieved in concert with some industrial development, whether a hydro dam or whatever, then departmental officials will work toward this end.
Some time ago departmental officials put forward an idea, and I stress an idea, in a discussion paper in which they visualized the possibility in certain circumstances of fish enhancement facilities amalgamated with low-head hydro dams, with the suggestion that such developments might be financed on a shared-cost basis. It was an idea put forward purely for discussion purposes so that the practicalities and the pros and cons could be considered in the broader context of salmon enhancement. There is nothing sinister about that. This kind of procedure happens all the time in government.
However, 1 should make it quite clear, particularly for the benefit of the hon. member for Skeena, that at this time potential projects combining fish enhancement and power generation have not been identified anywhere in B.C. I cannot say that the concept is dead. It remains in the development stage within the department and might well receive further consideration at some future date.
I believe that, in situations where there is no harm to salmon enhancement and where the benefits of salmon enhancement can be increased by the installation of a low-head dam, a serious look should be taken at that possibility by everyone, including all department officials.
Let me also remind hon. members that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has itself entered into the dam building business in areas where river or stream flow control is known to be a critical factor for fish. Such dams have proven highly successful in regulating water discharge for optimum fish production. To cite an example, this technique has been used in the Fulton River-maybe it was named after the hon. member-where a dam built by the department permits regulated water supplies to salmon spawning channels, and also in the Big Qualicum area to supply a spawning channel and hatchery complex.
These projects are both very successful fish producers which could not have been accomplished without dams providing controlled flow in the system. The point to be made here is that dams per se are not necessarily bad medicine as far as fish production is concerned. They can, and have been, used positively as a fish enhancement tool with good results.
At the same time I must also make it clear that the department remains committed to the natural production of fish, whenever and wherever possible, and to proper habitat protection measures.
High-head hydro dams can destroy salmon runs, in that they may present an impassable barrier to fish migrating upstream or downstream, as well as creating unnatural flow conditions which fundamentally change the aquatic environment in the area of the dam. It is the considered opinion of departmental experts that the various methods that have been tried to transport fish around such dams are not sufficiently successful to compensate for the numbers of fish that are frustrated in their migration patterns by the barrier. For this reason the department recognizes that fish, and large high-head hydro projects are essentially incompatible.
If I might enlarge a little on this subject, the Iskut-Stikine power project is a case in which B.C. Hydro is proposing a number of high dams capable of generating 2,765 megawatts of electricity, which could make it one of the largest power generators in the province. Considering that the Iskut-Stikine River system produces tens of thousands of salmon, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is naturally concerned about the environmental impact of such a project. Although the dams could be constructed above what is thought to be the natural upstream limit of migrating salmon, B.C. Hydro, with departmental input, has spent in the order of $1.25 million to $1.5 million over the past few years in biological studies alone to determine the downstream impact of the construction of the dams. Here again let me make the point very clear and unequivocal that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has no intention of approving a project which is likely to result in an unacceptable loss to the fisheries resource.
Turning to the wider question of the federal government's action and initiatives with regard to the west coast fisheries, I can confidently claim that the government's record is not one that we need be ashamed of. Rather, quite the contrary. I can point to a number of examples in support of this claim. The most obvious, perhaps, is the salmonid enhancement program, a federal-provincial project under which the federal government has undertaken to invest some $150 million over seven years with the objective of doubling the production of salmon and sea-run trout in British Columbia by the end of the next decade.
Back in 1975 when the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans first announced the salmonid enhancement program, he described it as "a bold and imaginative approach to the long-cherished dream of expanding our salmon resources". That was a very apt description because it has taken a considerable amount of boldness and more than a little imagination to plan and implement this major program, which involves the use of various enhancement techniques, including artificial spawning channels, hatcheries, fishways, lake fertilization and so forth.
It is now in its fifth year. The salmonid enhancement program is showing increasingly positive results in the number of salmon being produced through its various facilities throughout British Columbia. Last fall some 563 million eggs were obtained from the five species of salmon at SEP facilities.
May 28, 1981

Of this total, 69 million were incubated in artificial containers while the remainder, all of which are chum or sockeye, were developed in regulated stream or spawning environments. The projected production of salmon and steelhead trout to the fisheries, plus escapement, from the 1980 brood is in excess of
3.200.000	pieces. In a year when winter floods may have devasted large areas of natural spawn, it is reassuring that such large quantities of stocks are protected in hatcheries and other facilities. Looking ahead to 1984, the concluding year of phase one of the salmonid enhancement program, it is predicted that department-staffed facilities will have the capacity to provide additional adult returns of about 383,000 chum, 307,000 chinook, 243,000 coho, 1,010,000 pink, 4,000 sockeye,
5.000	cutthroat trout and 7,000 steelhead trout, or 1,959,000 pieces in all.
One of the very satisfying aspects of the program operation is the amount of solid support it has been given by the public at large in British Columbia. The federal and provincial governments' rallying cry to protect and enhance the salmon stocks has been taken up with great enthusiasm by young and old throughout the province, and at the present time there is a force of more than 6,000 volunteers working on various salmonid enhancement projects.
An economic analysis has predicted a cost-benefit ratio of about 1.3/1.0 for phase 1 of the salmonid enhancement program, with net national income benefits of around $120 million, in terms of 1980 dollars. In addition to these monetary advantages, one must also include other benefits in terms of employment, particularly benefiting native people, regional development and resource and environmental preservation, for which it is almost impossible to assess a value in dollar terms.
Some people may ask: why are you expending so much money and effort on salmon enhancement projects in B.C. when industrial concerns continue to pollute salmon rivers, such as the Fraser, or in one way or another destroy the habitat on which fish depend to breed and grow? That is a good question, and I hope people will not stop asking it.
The answer, however, is not a simple one. It involves complex and sensitive issues concerning levels of jurisdiction and the priorities one should accord to competing users of the water resource. As far as the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) is concerned, his mandate is quite clear: his responsibility, which, I might add, was decided by the Fathers of Confederation when Canada's statutes were first put together more than a century ago, is to protect and manage the fishery resource. And to further explain how he and his department views these obligations, I feel I could do no better than quote from a speech which the minister presented at the official opening a week or so ago of a $3.6 million hatchery at Puntledge on Vancouver Island, one of the salmonid enhancement program facilities to which I was referring a little earlier.
The minister made these remarks:
What we are discussing here is a renewable resource-one might say an eternal resource-belonging to the people of B.C. and Canada, and I feel it is a time to get tough. There must be a tougher approach on the part of the federal government to protect fish habitat and restore the salmon stocks to their previous
Hydro Development
levels of abundance. How tough should we get? My answer is tough enough to ensure proper planning to avoid disaster, to repair damaged areas, and the acceptance by all concerned of the real cost of development-to mitigate negative impact and restore to the fish and other wildlife a decent environment.
The Minister went on to say:
I am aware that in some quarters the department's resolve to fulfil its habitat protection obligations is viewed with some skepticism. Certainly we have not done all that we could or perhaps should have done, but for the record I should point out that over the past three years the department has laid some 74 charges in B.C. under the habitat sections of the Fisheries Act. These charges covered such abuses as the deposit of toxic contaminants, sedimentation, landfilling, gravel removal, oil spills and destructive logging practices.
Apart from instituting legal action, we have also taken firm positions on various environmental issues where fish are involved. One is the Quinsam coal development proposal. My officials are advising the company of our concerns regarding the possible impact of the mining operation on the Quinsam River and will identify three serious potential problem areas. Unless I can be fully assured that the fishery resources of the Quinsam will be adequately protected, I am not prepared to grant approval under the Fisheries Act for this development.
Another controversial issue on Vancouver Island concerns the discharge of toxic mine effluent into Buttle Lake, headwaters of the Campbell River. In this instance we have laid three charges against Western Mines and are insisting that the company clean up its mine disposal methods to safeguard the salmon resources of the Campbell River.
At this point it might be useful if I reiterated the department's objectives on fish habitat matters. They can be stated quite simply. First, there must be no net loss of productive fish habitat in locations where the federal government manages the fisheries. Second, where feasible, we will restore and develop areas to provide a net gain in the total amount of fish habitat. Third, we intend to be firm in the use of the federal statutory powers to protect fish habitat when and where necessary, temperd by co-operative, fair and reasonable dealings with those who seek to use the water resources for other purposes.
Certainly the department prefers to use the consultative, co-operation route to achieve results rather than wielding the big stick with the inevitable confrontations and court proceedings. However this is not an area where we can afford to procrastinate. Once a fish habitat is destroyed or a salmon stock wiped out, they cannot be magically replaced overnight just because we have been successful in a court prosecution, however heavy the fine. Even with everything working in our favour, it could take years to offset the damage caused by a careless river diversion, the building of a dam, the thoughtless dumping of fill in a marsh or spawning bed or the discharge of pollutants into fish-bearing waters. Often the damage is irreversible and valuable spawning or breeding areas may be lost forever.
It is ironic that it is in the mighty Fraser River, which has the greatest potential as a salmon producer of any river system in British Columbia and possibly in the world, that we are experiencing the most serious fish habitat losses. I suppose it is easy to say that those agencies which should have been looking out for the fish, whether they fall in the federal or provincial domain, have been lax in not living up to their responsibilities. Be that as it may, fish habitat continues to be lost and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is determined, one way or the other to reverse that trend. We cannot afford to wait.
It is not difficult to predict where the pressures on the Fisheries resource will originate in British Columbia in the near

May 28, 1981
Hydro Development
future. As readily available B.C. timber resources dwindle and harvesting moves to difficult terrain farther up river valleys, land slides or erosion problems are likely to occur to the detriment of entire streams.
On another front, with a projected hydro power deficit predicted in B.C. as early as 1985, one can anticipate renewed overtures seeking shared or primary use of major rivers to generate power. With current economic conditions encouraging an expansion of B.C. agricultural production, irrigation needs for new farm lands will become an even greater competitor with fish in the use of water. The mining industry- hardrock, placer and, most recently, coal-is also expanding dramatically and making its own unique demands on water resources. Finally, the prospect of greatly increased shipment of oil by tankers and the spectre of possible major oil spills poses another damage threat.
I know that departmental officials are working on these and other initiatives to improve and strengthen the department's management role on the west coast and elsewhere and, granted a reasonable degree of co-operation, I am sure their efforts will meet with success.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA HYDRO-JOINT FUNDING AND PROPOSED DAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the optimistic outlook presented by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Henderson) as to the commitment of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) to husbanding the environment of British Columbia, at least in so far as our salmon resource is concerned, one would have to wonder why the minister is hesitant about disclosing the documents which have been called for by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) in motion No. 28, which is a call for the production of correspondence, telegrams and other documents exchanged between the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and British Columbia Hydro, because if all the things the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has outlined are true, there ought to be nothing to hide.
I want to start by complimenting the hon. member for Skeena for bringing this very important matter before the House. It is in this type of forum that we can prevent in the future the kinds of disasters which have occurred far too often in British Columbia and in other parts of Canada in the past. However, in the comments of the hon. member for Skeena I found a hint that he feels there is something sinister in the fact that officials of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans would be meeting and corresponding with officials of British Columbia Hydro about the possibility of developing additional hydroelectric power on the streams of British Columbia.
I think the hon. member for Skeena typifies that overreaction to any environmental problem, which acts as a valuable conscience for our society but which sometimes makes it difficult for people to extract the facts and the truth from a lot of rhetoric and exaggeration. I am saying that this is an effective role for the hon. member for Skeena to play in serving as an environmental conscience, but as a former
professional person; a mechanical engineer, I believe man and nature can live in harmony. In fact, evidence shows that man can improve upon nature, and has in many ways, which makes our modern twentieth century civilization as comfortable as it is. Granted, there are problems and some disasters about which I want to say something, but I certainly agree with the hon. member for Skeena when he says that these documents should be available for public perusal. There ought to be nothing to hide, as I said a few moments ago.
I am glad the hon. member for Skeena said he was not opposed to the rational development of power on the waterways of British Columbia and in other parts of Canada because if we are to provide comfortable housing and meaningful employment for our young people who are to follow and if we are to feed the Third World nations and help them to develop their economies, we will have to develop our national resources in some manner in harmony with nature. However, we cannot avoid developing those resources and producing power as an important adjunct of that process.
The hon. member for Skeena seems to have constructed a very good case that there are certain documents in existence and that for some reason they are not being made available. When I was an alderman in a community in British Columbia, I had to deal with a very difficult problem. There was always a hue and cry as to whether documents should be made available or kept secret, and whether we should discuss things in camera or whether everything should be discussed before the public. I suggest that when planners are trying to lay out a framework for some concept of development, they ought to be free to do that, just as Members of Parliament sometimes, within the confines of caucus, like to talk and think out loud about concepts without having the pressure of public opinion on their backs. However, 1 submit that once documents relating to major developments of the scale we are talking about here are completed, printed, signed and exchanged between governments or departments, those documents should be made freely available. I do not know the reason for which the department and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans could argue to the contrary.
I recall in municipal politics that if one disclosed what he was thinking about too early, then outspoken and sometimes reactionary environmental groups would ascribe all kinds of motives and exaggerate excessively, to the point that a very good project might be stopped in its tracks even before the studies had been done to the extent rquired to make the case and to make it on sound technical and quantitative bases. On the other hand, if documents are withheld, then there is always the suspicion that somebody has something to hide or that there is a great conspiracy. There is always the danger, as we have seen in the Amax case in particular, that when the facts are known, it will be too late to reverse initiatives which have been taken because of the implications for employment or in the case of the Amax project at Alice Arm because of the implications for investment. There is always the danger that perhaps we will not find out until after our light bulbs are lit by a new hydroelectric dam, and then we will be so comfort-
May 28, 1981

able and dependent upon that new form energy that it will be absolutely impossible to reverse that situation.
I think the secret is to allow officials to carry out these interdepartmental or intergovernmental discussions, but at the point when documents are available, printed and signed, they must then be made available for debate in a parliamentary or democratic forum. Decisions on these proposals should never be made within the confines of the cabinet room or enacted by order in council. In cases of major studies which have an impact on the environment, the environmental assessment and review process should be mandatory in all cases. There should be a full process of public debate and discussion where the technical experts and environmentalists come together and the relative merits or lack of merits in these projects are debated.
In British Columbia there are some examples of environmental disaster. Many years ago British Columbia Hydro began to dam many of the valleys up above Vancouver without cutting down the trees. One notable example is the Stave Lake area where we constructed a reservoir, but it was just dotted with dead timber. That timber had a recoverable value, but at that time no one could be bothered to clear-cut the land first. The Bennett Dam in the Mackenzie area of northeastern British Columbia came about in the same way only about 12 years ago.
Vast areas of northeastern British Columbia were flooded without the trees being cut down first. There is a continuing debate about the elevation of the High Ross Dam in Washington State, which would flood a valley in southwestern British Columbia, the Skagit Valley, and there is great danger of eliminating a very valuable recreational area there. Everyone is very suspicious of the arrangements and the deals which were made with Seattle City Light and Power many years ago, which again was not done in the context of a parliamentary forum where everyone could witness the debate and hear all the pros and cons of the proposals.
Of course, the most remarkable example of lack of care about a major and important salmon spawning resource is the deterioration of the Fraser River system itself. In the lower reaches of the Fraser where I live in the Richmond-Delta area the coliform counts are so high that our children cannot swim there any longer. The good people of Vancouver who do not want to see any more development in our area, want to continue to expand their discharge of sewage into the Strait of Georgia and Fraser River. At some point it may well be too late to regenerate the Fraser River for the purpose of maintaining the salmon runs which are so essential to our economy and the way of life of the people of British Columbia.
However, I would like for a moment or two to speak on the positive side because, as the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, the benefits of the salmon enhancement program have been clearly demonstrated and, assuming the government maintains its commitment, we will see before five years have passed over $150 million invested directly in salmon enhancement projects. The Capilano hatchery, for anyone who has
Hydro Development
visited Vancouver, is a remarkable example of what man can do to improve upon nature and produce hundreds of thousands of salmon each year of the coho, chum and chinook varieties which will then return in two or four years. Almost without fishing boats those salmon can be trapped back at the hatchery as they return to spawn and produce another cycle. That is essentially a man-made contrivance which has improved on nature many, many times over to our advantage.
The spawning channels at the hatcheries at Qualicum and Little Qualicum, have proven to be a tremendous improvement on nature where eggs laid by female salmon are nurtured and regenerate many, many times more efficiently than in the natural environment. The Puntledge River hatchery on Vancouver Island is an example of a hatchery being built immediately below a hydroelectric dam. In fact, it is an attempt to co-ordinate hydroelectric development with salmon enhancement in a positive way. It has its shortcomings, but many of the improvements technology is providing, such as vertical slot fishways and the ability to fertilize the lakes and reservoirs upstream of the dam as is done at Great Central lake on Vancouver Island, and the fish ladder and hatchery operations at Hell's Gate in the Fraser Canyon, provide the opportunity for salmon to multiply and coexist with man so that we might enjoy an increasing benefit in terms of the food resource that that represents to us all.
So I am saying that these sorts of projects should not be ruled out without detailed study which has to start somewhere, and I would be astounded if the hon. member for Skeena wanted B.C. Hydro to do such studies in isolation. I would suggest it is probably a tremendous advantage that they are meeting with DFO and provincial government officials, and consulting section 33 of the Fisheries Act. Without this kind of consultation, Mr. Speaker, the kind of disasters that have occurred in the past might well reoccur in the future. So although the hon. member for Skeena is serving as a valuable whistle blower, and I agree with him wholeheartedly that these documents should be released at this point, there is also, I think, a responsible position for the minister to take, provided, of course, the government will comply with this motion and release these documents because I do not see that it has anything to hide.
The Amax controversy and the cessation of the discharge from that mine site today should probably teach us all some lessons. It will teach the investors, the entrepreneurs and the industrialists something about the increased public consciousness and concern for environmental questions. But again, to add some balance I would suggest that the mere existence of a plume, which was discovered yesterday in Alice Arm, does not prove that there is a hazard to fish life or man. I do not know whether the hon. member for Skeena drags on those plumes with which we have to contend in committee rooms but many people do and plumes, whether they be from cigarettes or tall smoke stacks at places like Sudbury, are a fact of life. Man will continue to produce effluents and discharges so long as the natural biological processes continue. The mere existence of a plume should not be cause in itself for people to go parading

around with placards and overreacting. The question is: does the plume in Alice Arm really carry on outside Alice Arm, which would be contrary to the special permit that was issued, and are the concentrations of particulates in excess of the limits set out under the legislation? In that case there is definitely a hazard, and I think the fact that Amax has agreed to cease the discharge means they are now concerned that there may indeed be a problem, that their hydraulic studies were not done thoroughly enough and their modelling of the situation did not simulate the real circumstances in Alice Arm.
So I believe that development is essential, and I think the hon. member for Skeena agrees with that. Much as people in his riding may not enjoy all the amenities those in Vancouver, Toronto or Ottawa enjoy, I would not want him to suggest that the people in the Skeena area, Prince Rupert, Terrace and elsewhere should not be able to aspire to the same types of comforts that our modern industrial society is providing. Perhaps in the long run, if we in this party agree to the favourite notion of the NDP, that we should have an industrial development strategy for Canada in order to have more finished product from our resources, we will have to contend with some of the large-scale projects such as the one at Hat Creek and chemical plants and factories, steel mills, and who knows what else. All I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that I believe, and history will show, that if the engineering is done properly, if foresight is applied and there is an open process of studying these concepts and proposals, we can improve upon the natural circumstances. So let us keep a sense of balance on these questions.
I am not convinced that the hon. member for Skeena's notion of lowhead type turbines will sove the problem because there are economies of scale associated with transmission systems and networks that may mitigate against these lowhead type turbines unless they are going to serve merely a small neighbourhood area. In fact, I think we can build large scale projects in harmony with nature and in the process improve on the environment as far as our biological resources are concerned. I realize that other hon. members would like to have a chance to speak. I understand this debate will go on for another 20 or 30 minutes, so I will resume my seat at present and conclude by saying that 1 hope the government will accede to the request of the hon. member for Skeena.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and motions Nos. 1 and 3 (Mr. Blenkarn).

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as always I feel privileged to speak in this assembly; this evening particularly so because we are debating a most important bill, Bill C-57, to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to provide for a revenue tax in respect of petroleum and gas.
This bill is intended to increase substantively the revenues of the federal government by new taxation of those sectors of the Canadian economy which are growing, primarily the publishing, cosmetics, tobacco, alcohol and energy industries. This is being done at a time when the economy should receive a boost through tax reduction and decreased government spending policies such as those being followed in the United States, rather than tax increases.
Before speaking more specifically on various aspects of the bill, and in particular on part IV cited as the petroleum and gas revenue tax act, I want to address myself more generally to the present nature of the Canadian economy and the government's response to it.
Recently, the government has stated repeatedly that it is following a policy of economic gradualism. I ask: gradualism in what? Gradualism in the rate of rise in inflation which has
May 28, 1981

reached 12.6 per cent? Gradualism in the rate of rise of bankruptcies in the Canadian economy? In the first quarter of this year business bankruptcies are already up by 30 per cent over the comparable quarter last year. Is it gradualism in the rate of rise of government spending over the last few years which has now reached astronomical annual deficits of some $14 billion or $15 billion? Gradualism in the rate of change of the money supply? Gradualism in the rate of rise in interest rates? The wild gyrations in interest rates both up and down in the last year are hardly extremes of economic gradualism. Is it gradualism in taxation of selected growth industries such as are implicit in Bill C-57? The federal government is now seeking revenues from areas which have traditionally belonged to the provinces-taxation of resources at the source, a form of royalty. Mr. Speaker, I ask you, gradualism in what? Just what economic levers available to it has the government shifted gradually? Indeed, just what economic levers does the national government control today?
The government can increase the levels of taxation, as it is doing with this bill, Bill C-57. We have today in the Canadian economy the gradualism of confusion and economic acquiescence to forces beyond the control or fiscal management of this government brought about by a decade of economic neglect and misdirection. This national government has lost the ability to manage the national economy, lost it partially to the provinces. By de facto royalty taxation of resources, it is trying to regain some of that lost control. The government has lost it to the dictates of international economic forces beyond its control. It has lost it to the built up inertia and momentum of its own spending habits and policies during the last decade, policies directed toward wealth, redistribution with little or no attention to wealth formation and the competitive productivity of Canada's work force. In productivity we have dropped from second place to twelfth place in the last decade among the nations of the world. This bill, more than any other government measure, highlights the mess in which the Canadian economy finds itself today.
Canadian interest rates are totally at the mercy of the levels established in the United States of America. Why have the U.S. rates reached such levels and are apparently being maintained there, rates which have caused alarm to world leaders such as Helmut Schmidt? Why are U.S. rates so high, in excess of 20 per cent, when, indeed, the most recent monthly inflation rates were of the order of 5 per cent? There is a 15 per cent spread, Mr. Speaker. Has Canada made representations or asked to be apprised of the need for such high U.S. rates? Is the United States following economic gradualism? The U.S. dollar is fundamentally the basis or standard of all other free-world currencies. Why then are U.S. rates so high when its inflationary rate is reasonable? The United States is pursuing a course of reasserting its leadership role in the world. What better way to proceed than to strengthen its currency, promote an influx of investment capital, permit capital accumulation such that it can be directed for hard commercial and needed industrial reinvestment rather than frivolous consumer indulgence? This is not a policy of gradual-
Excise Tax
ism in the United States, it is economic shock treatment. In all its ferocity it is being imposed on Canada and Canadians; and this government recognizes, literally admits, that the economic mess it has created over a decade is so severe that about all it can do is pray that the U.S. will relent and reduce the severity of the shock treatment and lower interest rates. The government must have prayed pretty hard because today there came some small relief and interest rates dropped slightly.
Our very own spending habits; causing us to live well beyond our means-and effectively off the backs of future generations, have rendered us impotent. So we bring forth Bill C-57 and set back a vibrant oil and gas industry for at least a decade so that the government can generate a little more revenue to keep the deficit from rising a little higher. What can we do? We can face up squarely and realistically to the mess we are in and begin to plan, seriously plan, for the mid-term and the longer term while holding the economy together as best we can in the short term.
This nation needs an energy agreement, not only with one province but with all it needs it now. This nation needs an industrial strategy, and it needs one soon. Not an industrial strategy based on a dollar which must be constantly propped up by frantic fiscal transactions by the national government and the Bank of Canada, but a strategy based upon a dollar which has been allowed to assume its true international value. This nation needs a new rationale, a new direction, difficult as it may be, toward government spending and regulation at all levels of government. Government must manage the national economy more and be involved in it less.
In 1978, after a series of federal-provincial sectoral meetings, followed by a first ministers' conference on the Canadian economy, major decisions on the economy were agreed upon. What were those decisions and how do they differ from the government's fiscal and economic measures of today, which are more taxation and more spending, as is evident by the bill before us?
I want to refer to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau), analysis of the economy in 1978, just three years ago. This is what he told the first ministers:
Allow me to set out for a few moments what I believe are necessary conditions in this new partnership. Amongst many, I believe four are of primary importance:
First, it is governments' task (in consultation with Canadians) to establish the economic goals the country can achieve-
What are these goals today? More taxation? To continue:
Second, we must understand that private citizens and private markets have the major task in ensuring economic performance in Canada.
Not the government, the private sector. The Prime Minister went on to say:
Our job in government is to provide an economic framework-we cannot and should not manage all the details of economic activity.
What is this economic framework today? He said:
Third, we must recognize the country is diverse in its regions and that the economies of each region are continuously changing. It is because Canada is diverse and dynamic, that the relations between governments at all levels must be flexible and adaptable. That we must also demonstrate.

May 28, 1981
Excise Tax
Demonstrate how? By punishing the west through damaging resource taxation.
The fourth point the Prime Minister made at that first ministers' conference was:
-good economic performance is not an end in itself. But without it, the kind of country we all want, humane, tolerant and compassionate, is not possible. Therefore, we must provide the effective leadership which good economic performance demands. At the same time, as political leaders, we must aim to serve Canadians in a variety of ways, not just to help manage the balance sheet.
Where is that leadership today, Mr. Speaker? The Prime Minister went on to say:
From 1965 to 1975, government expenditures, at all levels, grew from 26 per cent to 36 per cent of our gross national product.
There are many who argue that our governments have grown too fast and too large. They say that in our attempts to provide government services for people, we sacrificed economic efficiency and competitiveness. I have some sympathy with this point of view.
That was his view in 1968. He said:
I recognize, as we all must, that if we are not efficient and competitive, if we do not create wealth in the country, we cannot sustain our efforts to help those who need it and build a more humane and equitable society.
But what have we done and what are we now doing?
The Prime Minister also said:
Our aim must be to constrain the growth of our governments. We must reduce our share of gross national product. But, even more important, we must reduce the intrusion of bureaucracy in the daily lives of Canadians.
That is what the Prime Minister said in 1978 at a first ministers' conference. What does this bill do? Is is an imposition, an intrusion in the taxation areas of other levels of government, particularly in the resource areas. The discussion culminated at that conference, and it is time we had another economic ministers' conference. There is need today for a first ministers' conference on the economy, and it should have been held several months ago. That conference concluded along these notes:
The first ministers of Canada's eleven governments have arrived at far-reaching agreement in a large number of economic matters.
Following three days of intensive meetings in Ottawa and two months of preparatory sectoral talks, they announced steps today that will:
-facilitate the setting of economic objectives-
What are those today?
-improve demand management policies,-
I will want to refer to these in a minute.
-foster responsible price and incomes behaviour,
-strengthen the business investment climate,-
This should be achieved not through more taxation, but through less taxation.
-and further shape trade, industry, energy, manpower and regional development initiatives.
First ministers see an expanding private sector as the major impetus for growth in the Canadian economy.
My, how this differs from the massive throttling of the Canadian economy through the National Energy Program and its fall-out legislation such as Bill C-57 and Bill C-48! What
were those demand management policies? There are three of them:
(i)	The general instruments of monetary and fiscal policy should be used to encourage the growth of demand which would bring the desired growth of output and employment at declining rates of inflation.
(ii)	The monetary policy being pursued by the Bank of Canada is consistent with this objective.
It was consistent at that time.
Is it consistent today?
First ministers agreed that the Governor of the Bank of Canada should review the objectives of monetary policy with the conference of finance ministers on an annual basis.
When was the last time the Governor of the Bank of Canada met with the finance ministers of the various governments in this country? Third:
(iii)	The trend of government expenditure growth should be held, on average, to less than the trend growth in the value of the GNP or provincial gross product.
Is that what we have done in the last year?
In this context, however, it was agreed that capital expenditures of a revenue producing nature were important to economic growth and development.
My, how these policies differ and how they are at variance with the policies of the government and the Governor of the Bank of Canada just three years later! What has happened during this period? I will tell Your Honour what has happened. We have not contained our spending as governments in this land. In particular, the federal government has continued to spend, and spend some more, and increase the national debt until we now know that that debt is over $14 billion per year and that much of it must be refinanced at much higher interest rates. So, we bring in a bill, Bill C-57, to tax primarily the growing industries in this land, particularly energy.
I find the 8 per cent tax, which is called the resource royalty tax, to be particularly interesting because, to my mind, that tax has several objectives; not only to raise revenue for a faltering government which is broke, and is in debt up to its ears, but to take revenue from the energy companies in western Canada and lower their cash flow to such a level of insignificance that they will start to put terrific pressure on the provincial governments to lower their royalties. That tax of 8 per cent is the federal government's way of imposing resource control, even though it does not have constitutional power to do so, or imposing a resource royalty on the provincial resource when there is no room for that taxation. So, the federal government simply said: "We will take from the companies their cash flow and tell them to go to the provinces and have them lower their royalties so the companies' cash flow can be increased".
That was essentially the reply of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to an hon. member on this side of the House who asked about the solution to the problem of wells which were being shut down in Saskatchewan. The minister said to go and ask the province to lower their royalties. So this is doing something indirectly through the Constitution which cannot be done directly.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel a sense of deja vu, in rising to speak on this bill today. Over 200 years ago the Americans staged a tea party in Boston to protest against representation without taxation. That is precisely what we are again now talking about right here.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext: It was the other way around!

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
The government is asking Parliament to give carte blanche approval to a bill which would automatically increase excise taxes indexed to the consumer price index. How convenient it would be for the government not to have to face Parliament when future taxes are increased! How convenient it would be for the government not to have to deal again with unpopular measures in the future! But that is not the Canadian way because it was not the American way. It is the Liberal way. I have been present religiously in this House since Parliament was convened over a year ago and I have not seen one positive measure put forward by this government-not one piece of legislation which adds to the productivity of this country. That is what the free enterprise system is all about.
This bill is oppressive, regressive, rotten, and imposes risk-stifling taxation. It is putting an 8 per cent tax on our gas industry. Hon. members opposite stand up so proudly and say this is Canadianization. They call it a national oil policy, but I call it a disgrace and a nationalization oil policy. Not one piece of progressive legislation which deals with building Canada or measures to get this moribund economy moving again and put Canadians back to work, not out of work, has been offered.
This legislation is regressive, oppressive, unfair, discriminatory and will only add to the cost of living and inflationary woes of one of the greatest nations in the world. It is crippling the citizens of Canada.
We do not need negative legislation. We need positive measures which will provide social justice and groceries at a reasonable cost. We need jobs. That is what my constituents are interested in. We need less unemployment, not more. We need lower interest rates, and it can be done, so that more Canadians can carry on their small businesses and afford mortgages so they can own their own homes. It is the Canadian dream, if you will.
We need positive action and some sign from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), who smirks and smiles and shrugs, that he is aware that inflation is enemy number one in this country. We need positive measures to encourage the manufacturing sector and to stimulate R and D.
Most of all we need an awareness on the part of the government that the economy is sluggish and that its policies are mainly to blame and should be changed. They can be changed.
I am fortunate to have a wonderful corporate citizen in my constituency in Molson's Brewery, one of the largest breweries in the world. The new rate of excise tax on beer goes far beyond the Crosbie budget in terms of the application of the
Excise Tax
levy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Deputy Prime Minister-the alleged-and I say alleged-Minister of Finance, have launched a new beer on the market. I wonder how many members opposite have heard about it. It is called "Overdraft". It is not a popular seller. It does not go down well with the average Canadian, like Molson's. Like the government, Overdraft is full of froth and suds and foam. I resent the government's end run in indexing this beer excise tax to the alcoholic beverages subgroup of the consumer price index.
I resent periodic increases in this tax without reference to this Parliament. We have not had the Boston tea party yet. Like some of my colleagues who spoke earlier, I am saying we have not had it

yet.
I resent the ham-handed efforts of the government to avoid facing Parliament on this issue in the future. I resent its arrogance-read any newspaper and you will see it-in attempting for all time to stave off the politically risky business of dealing with increases in the price of beer in future budgets.
The opposition was told that this tax is being imposed to protect government revenues derived from this tax from erosion and that it was based on the same formula which applied to the indexation of personal income tax. What a joke. Indexation of personal income tax is designed to protect the taxpayer from inflation and to discipline government to better manage our fiscal affairs. It was not intended that the government should ever profit from inflation by automatically receiving higher revenues from people because they obtained cost of living increases to ward off the ravages of the record high inflation which has been brought on by this government. That evidence is based on statistics, it is not just my opinion.
By indexing taxes on beer the government is doing or attempting to do exactly and precisely the opposite of what indexation of personal income tax, as originally suggested by the Hon. Robert Stanfield, is doing-it is taking advantage of a formula which is meant to buffer the consumer against inflation and fiscal management.
If we allow this measure to pass, the government will be allowed to tax people on inflation and to do it without ever again referring the matter to Parliament. Shades of the Constitution-shades of metric!
I am sure all hon. members are familiar with the brief which was sent to all Members of Parliament by the Brewers Association of Canada.
I would like to quote from a letter I received from a driver-supervisor for Brewer's Retail in my home city of Barrie. This is a concerned Canadian, not some executive officer. He points out that with this insidious and ad valorem tax on beer, by 1991 a case of 24 beer will cost $23.64 and a bottle of gin will cost $16.64. He writes:
I find this hard to understand since the alcohol content of distilled spirits is higher by volume by 35 per cent than it is in beer, I am also concerned that the proposal of automatic increases on alcoholic beverages would not require the approval of Parliament.
