speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate on Bill C-57 it is significant to note that from the earliest of times, in terms of the parliamentary system, the public, represented by their elected representatives, has been very jealous of the control by government of the taxation of the citizen. It is accordingly with some regret that we note that the system implanted permanently within the tax framework, as established by Bill C-57, has the effect of removing that direct participation by members of Parliament in determining what the tax laws of the day shall be.
Before my colleagues to the left scream that this is the very thing that has happened recently in the province of Ontario in the recent provincial budget, let me say I agree, and the comments I have in respect of this government will apply
equally to any government which endeavours to impose tax without presenting to the elected representatives of the Parliament or legislature to which they belong an opportunity to discuss and vote for or against a particular piece of legislation.
I do not think it matters whether the government is provincial, federal, Conservative or Liberal, or in an unusual circumstance, NDP, and I say "unusual circumstance" because fortunately the country has had so few of them.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext: Go west.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests I go west. I have been west. The great people of western Canada had an opportunity to get rid of a canker that had infested them in British Columbia, and hopefully that kind of circumstance will not recur.
In any event I think it is appropriate that members of this House have regard for the change that is occurring. That change is not one we should accept without very substantial and recognized complaint. We have seen changes in this place in respect of our ability to stand and speak for or against a particular issue; changes in such innocuous pieces of legislation as the Canada-Germany Tax Convention which contains a provision by which there is no legislative enactment, in respect of changes, without the imposition of closure, which is built into the very piece of legislation presented to the House and subsequently passed. This is the same kind of creeping undemocratic authoritarianism about which all members should be concerned.
The provisions of Bill C-57 go far beyond that and that alone. They permit the growth of an element in our economy, sought allegedly to be retarded by the government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) just the other day, in a very learned dissertation on what the psychology of inflation entailed, indicated that some people believe that because prices are going to increase, it is appropriate that those people increase the price of their product or their services. In the process, they increase those prices in excess of what is really required. Of course, those people of whom he spoke include the members of his own cabinet who have brought before the House this piece of legislation.
It is the personification of the inflation psychology which drives prices up, and this is allegedly opposed by the government. Yet, because of the way in which it fixed its ever-increasing tax bite in respect of excise taxes, it is clear that by fixing them, in relation to certain products covered by the Act, to an element of the consumer price index, the government has given a clear signal to the entire population of Canada that it expects the consumer price index, as it relates to those elements, to increase. The government has made an announcement to Canadians generally that tomorrow the prices of those goods will be higher than today. How has the government made that announcement? It did so by suggesting that its revenues be tied to the prices as they increase.
An ad valorem tax would similarly go down in the event that the price of the commodity, as an element of the consumer price index, was reduced. Of course, the government knows
May 28, 1981

that the price is not coming down because the government is the greatest cause of inflation in the nation. What it has done now, having caused inflation, is to tie its tax grab to the inflationary spiral it has created. Beyond that, it has then gone to the public and announced that prices tomorrow will be higher than prices today.
We know the effect of that kind of inflation psychology. It drives the prices of products out of the reach of the ordinary Canadian. It has the effect, naturally, of influencing the ultimate cost of money. Interest rates have skyrocketed. Despite the fact that today they may have taken a brief dip- and I hope it is not the kind of dip that occurred last year which was followed by insurmountable increases, and presumably we will not be bereaved of those high rates for some time-the fact of the matter is that as a result of increasing inflationary pressure, interest rates will and must rise. It is illogical to ever assume that the investor, whoever that investor may be, the bank or the individual, is prepared to lend his or her money, in the case of the bank its money, at a rate of return which is less than the rate at which the money is being eroded by inflation. With an inflation rate of 13 per cent, it is unrealistic to expect interest rates at 10 per cent.
As a matter of fact, if you really analyse what is occurring, in the event that a lender is in the 50 per cent bracket, a rate of interest at 18 per cent will result in a net return of 9 per cent, and inflation is eating away at the equity of a loan at the rate of 13 per cent, so the loan in fact will result in an annual loss of 4 per cent in terms of the real value of the capital amount of the loan.
Interest rates have to be tied to something more basic than what the government has suggested, that is a direct connection with the U.S. rates, having regard to the fact that every Thursday we have been artificially manipulating interest rates in Canada through the purchase of treasury bills.
Those prices have, in large measure, been influenced by a determination not to permit the Canadian dollar to decline at a rate which would startle the public into realizing what a horrendous mess the government has made of the economy of our country. The real value of the dollar should not be sustained as a consequence of interest rates but, rather, through the value of the product itself and, like any other commodity, if it is in demand, as it should be, instead of being something which is sold off to acquire another product in a foreign currency which may produce a higher interest rate-if it is, accordingly, in demand for some other purpose than for the generation of interest alone-then that commodity, that dollar, will be sought after and have an intrinsic value. How can that intrinsic value be established in the massive amounts which are required for the purposes of today's economy? It is very clear that the most effective and direct way by which this can be done is through the development in western Canada of our gigantic resources which will contribute to our energy requirements.
Excise Tax
Why am I dealing with that issue now? Very clearly, because this delightful piece of legislation has the very opposite effect. It has a provision with respect to a special royalty imposed against the generation of energy revenues, a special tax not based upon profit but, rather, upon recovery of an amount. It is a gross tax, a royalty tax, new and special and designed, I say, to retard development which is essential not just for that part of the country but for the whole nation.
Accordingly, I submit that the only way we can avoid the economic calamities which are caused in our country as a direct result of high interest rates is to attract Canadian investment into an area which is absolutely vital. Those dollars, once tied up in plant and machinery, not only in that part of the country which will ultimately use it but also in that part of the country expanding its economy in order to produce the goods which are needed, will not be available to flee the country in search of a higher interest rate in the United States or elsewhere but will be used for the purpose of generating, as genuine equity, the kind of energy production that is required and vital to Canadian needs.
I was interested in the fact that this ad valorem concept which is built into Bill C-57 has not gone unnoticed among the general public. I had occasion to meet with a constituent who is astounded and offended by the fact that this government would introduce a piece of legislation designed to preclude Parliament from examining on a regular basis the tax structure of the country. I had thought that that kind of consideration was one which might arouse the ire of people in this House and might generally concern some theoretician who likes to examine parliamentary history, but it appears that that is not the case. People are genuinely concerned about the protection of their rights, and they look to this House to protect those rights. They look to the members of this House to undertake that task and lead the way so that other governments, be they provincial or otherwise, come to recognize that the public is not asleep. The public is not prepared to have its rights trampled upon. I refer to those rights which historically have been the foundation of our very being here and the very foundation of the system which we currently enjoy. Accordingly, it is appropriate that we direct as much attention to this issue as we can, hoping-and I am concerned having regard to the way in which the government has responded in the past- to make them realize that something fundamental and wrong is being perpetrated upon not only the system but also the people who live by it and suffer from it.
If I may just return for a moment to the issue of the detrimental effect of the resource royalty tax of 8 per cent upon the general economy of the nation, I might add that I find it extremely strange to learn that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is about to prepare the public for another increase in the price of petroleum products at the pump. He is telling us now that we shall shortly be paying an additional two and a quarter cents a gallon to be added to the two and a quarter cents a gallon we have already paid for a total of four and a half cents a gallon. The reason is that Alberta is reducing its oil production by another 60,000

May 28, 1981
Excise Tax
barrels a day and by September, presumably, will reduce it by another 60,000 barrels a day, with the result that at that time, if the federal government follows the policy it has already announced and implemented, a total of 6.75 cents a gallon will be imposed by way of special taxes for the purpose of paying for imported foreign oil to make up for the deficit in production capacity which Canada, chiefly through Alberta, has been able to make available to the general public.
It is curious that this government can extract potentially 6.75 cents a gallon from the public by way of a special tax and pay that money directly to foreign producers of petroleum products, but it could not take that same 6.75 cents and pay it to another Canadian. There has never been a suggestion by the government that the method it has adopted for the purpose of paying for this increased price of petroleum should not be applied in settling its disputes with the government of Alberta. Yet the mechanism is there, and I am convinced, as surely as I stand here, that when that dispute is resolved, the government will have fixed permanently as a tax, never to be removed, the 4.5 cents or the 6.75 cents, whatever it may be, because once imposed, tax is used for whatever purpose the government may set about to use it.
I attended a meeting of the Public Accounts Committee this morning. We had before us the deputy minister of national revenue, and we were discussing those Canadian taxpayers who have never filed tax returns. It was suggested that some of them might well have been in the over-65 age group. I explained at the time that the reason for that particular group's declining to pay tax is probably that they remember that in 1918 when the act was introduced, the government of the day promised that it was simply going to be temporary in nature and, accordingly, they are holding the government to its word.
It is absolutely vital that we come to recognize that this piece of legislation is damaging in its present form, and it is damaging for the reasons I have discussed with respect to the effect it has upon the democratic system, our right to be consulted and our right to speak on and vote for or against a tax increase. It is inappropriate that this House should be asked to grant permanently to the government the right to extract taxes on an ever-escalating basis.
It is wrong because it has no regard to the fact that the greatest way to build the country is by removing, not imposing, additional taxes on the great energy resources available which, if developed, will remedy the economic ills with which we are concerned.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-57 and Bill C-48 are the main component parts of the October 28, 1980 budget or, as the government now prefers to call it, their National Energy Program. Provisions of both bills and their implications that are now so apparent are a major irritant and a source of extreme frustration leading to serious alienation throughout all of western Canada but especially in Alberta. This extremely serious situation must surely have been obvious
to every member of Parliament about two weeks ago when the 126 oil and gas well servicing industry representatives spent two days in Ottawa. Their very effective lobby cannot be dismissed if only because they were all Canadian managers and owner-operators of the entire petroleum service industry in Alberta. They were effective because they were all speaking from personal experience about severe cutbacks, lay-offs, current massive budget reductions, idle drilling rigs and supporting services. They were all having to face the reality of a vastly reduced level of operation or perhaps complete shutdown which would lead to selling out or moving to the United States. Those were the grim realities that faced a good many of them, and surely the grim message they brought cannot be ignored, especially by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
Of the two energy bills this one, Bill C-57, is the more important for the oil and gas well servicing sector, and for me personally because of my special interest and concerns in natural gas in southern Alberta. The discovery and use of natural gas took place about 100 years ago near my home city of Medicine Hat. As a natural resource, natural gas has made a major contribution to that city, and the industrial development of gas-related industries contributed significantly to our painfully slow recovery from the lost generation of the drought and depression wracked 1930s. That was followed by another ten years of recovery and readjustment. Natural gas has rightfully been part of our heritage for almost 100 years. Both of these taxes, the production tax, also known as the natural gas and gas liquids tax, and the 8 per cent wellhead tax known as the PGRT, are viewed with extreme shock and bitter disappointment by all of us in southern Alberta. All Albertans are completely convinced that they are a deliberate and massive federal revenue grab directed right at Alberta.
It was my privilege to participate as a member of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs whenever discussions and witnesses relating to natural gas issues were before that committee. I wish to express my thanks and appreciation to the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) for their analysis of the separate representations of the various witnesses before the committee and those received by letter. The first submission to the committee was from my home city of Medicine Hat which was presented by mayor Ted Grimm and alderman Dr. Ken Sauer, who stressed their quite unique situation wherein the city has developed and owned its own natural gas and electric utilities for almost 100 years during which time these utilities have been exempt from corporate, income, production and sales taxes.
The application of these taxes has been described in their brief quite aptly as confiscatory, abnormal and constitutionally without precedent. They pointed out:
-we do not export the resource-
That is, natural gas:
-nor the profits from its exploitation. We upgrade the resource in Canada, thereby creating jobs for Canadians.
May 28, 1981

Later on in this logical and common sense comment they had this to say:
A court of law may interpret the legal technicalities and find that the tax is unconstitutional, but only Parliament can interpret the fairness or equity of taxation.
The new taxes will boost Medicine Hat's residential gas rates by 197.6 per cent, surely an increase much higher than at any other point in Canada. The minister's appraisal was that:
The gas tax is a uniform absolute amount for all gas users and thus customers in all parts of Canada will face the same increases in absolute costs.
I must say that comment is small comfort indeed to retired people in Medicine Hat when they pay next winter's gas heating bills.
Now another witness before that committee was the Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops Ltd., and they made two visits to Ottawa to tell their story of the impact of this tax on rural Alberta. They ably represent 85 user member-owned rural utilities who supply 40,000 natural gas services for 140,000 people in rural Alberta. They operate a 40,000 mile distribution system which supplies about 80 per cent of Alberta's rural areas. They made the statement that:
Time will show that it was, and continues to be, sound planning to convert to the more plentiful natural gas, from the depleting and more costly portable fuels such as oii and propane.
And the gas co-op has extended a very generous offer to other provinces in Canada to share their experiences and expertise in rural gasification developments. They also make two telling points respecting the impact of these two taxes. The first is that substantially higher gas costs due to the taxes will be a severe deterrent to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources natural gas conversion program now under way. That program is logical and sound. However, this tax approach is surely not the way to go about it.
The second impact is the immediate and enormous cost increases of commercial fertilizers, most of which use natural gas feedstocks in addition to those other farm fuel costs. In total, it must be obvious that our basic food production costs will increase significantly.
Another witness, the Bow River Gas Co-op, a federation member with headquarters at Vauxhall, Alberta, has illustrated these cost increases with recent figures in a report dated January 7, 1981. On 136,000 mechanically irrigated acres, the cost increases due to the new taxes are as follows: For natural gas used as a fuel in irrigation pumping, a total of $174,000; for two varieties of fertilizers, 11-5-5 and 34-0-0, a total of $659,000, for a total cost increase of $835,000, all due to the natural gas taxes alone. And that figure prompted this appropriate comment from that co-op.
This is one big sum of tax money to take out of one small farming community.
The Bow River Gas Co-op concluded its cost statement by indicating:
If we farmers are not given any protection against this special tax on all fuels, I know there will be a drastic drop in production on irrigated farms.
That statement was made by one of its executives, a man by the name of Henry J. Dick.
Excise Tax
The Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops Ltd. made a very reasonable suggestion that an extension of time be allowed for the tax payment from the current 30 days, after the end of the month of sale, to 90 days. This was a very reasonable suggestion; I think it was widely supported in committee. However, the minister in his appraisal suggested that other taxpayers could also make similar claims and that to extend the time of payment of the tax to all taxpayers would be costly in terms of lost revenue. Surely the minister has missed their point completely. It is a very valid point and should be reconsidered.
Another witness was the Alberta Energy Services Association. This is the energetic group to which I referred in my opening comments who were here about two weeks ago. That 126-member lobby represented the oil and gas well servicing industry from such widely separated places as: Red Deer, Drayton Valley, Whitecourt, Lloydminster, Calgary, Brooks, Medicine Hat, Weyburn, Estevan and Swift Current.
As Canadian citizens and as responsible electors-and this is their phrasing-they questioned the government energy policy which results in thousands of lost jobs, increasing reliance on very costly foreign oil and financial instability in numerous small communities such as the ones I have just indicated. They also pointed out that hundreds of wells producing less than 12 barrels per day have been made uneconomical by the National Energy Program. Such wells are particularly service-intensive and contribute to energy self-sufficiency throughout Canada, no matter where they are.
The Canadian Petroleum Association in its committee presentation confirmed that Alberta indeed has surplus and proven natural gas supplies of between 16 and 20 trillion cubic feet in capped gas wells. But they are concerned with the continued and increasing slowdown in both drilling and exploration as a result of the National Energy Program, while at the same time the government is pushing its gas conversion program to utilize those capped gas well supplies. I think they have reason to be concerned. They reminded us all that five to ten years' lead time is necessary for adequate exploration and development planning.
The companion association, the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, was critical of the National Energy Program grant system which heavily favours investment on federal lands, whereas their members are largely confined to the western Canadian sedimentary basin in the provinces. They said bluntly that both taxes should be withdrawn.
The Alberta Chamber of Commerce reaffirmed its belief that Canada can achieve energy self-sufficiency through prompt development of Canada's domestic energy resources, particularly oil. The chamber of commerce bluntly said that the production and wellhead taxes constitute a major infringement by the federal government on the rights of the provinces to own and control their natural resources. They concluded by saying:
A preferable course would be for the federal government to proceed under the Income Tax Act, and if justifiable, consider establishing a surtax on income deemed to be windfall profit.

May 28, 1981
Excise Tax
In concluding my remarks pertaining to the submissions before the standing committee, I must say that I very much appreciated the somewhat more favourable appraisal of the Minister of Finance respecting two odd groups. One was the Motorcycle and Moped Industry Council and the other was the Canadian Water Well Association. Needless to say, the comments were a nice change of pace from most of his other discouraging words on just about all other submissions.
In conclusion, I say very seriously that throughout these remarks I have only repeated several references by others concerning the propriety and legality of the production tax and the PGRT, but surely this is the bottom line of the entire National Energy Program, at least as perceived by the west, especially by Alberta. Let there be no misunderstanding. I am referring to that threat to Alberta's natural resources by the federal Liberal government in these two particular taxes, as well as in Bill C-48. There is a valid reason for what is happening in the west right now. It makes little difference whether we call it alienation, frustration, anger or even separation. These emotions are very real and exist in Alberta, essentially because of the perceived threat to our natural resources which we have only owned and controlled since 1930-that is only 51 years ago!
At this moment the unanimous decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal is still the law of the land, at least until it is overturned by a higher level, the Supreme Court of Canada. Until that happens, surely the Alberta position applies, at least in so far as that decision is defined.
Finally, I am sure the Minister of Finance, his parliamentary secretary and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) are aware of this feeling in the west and its relationship to this particular bill. I say to them that the 135 amendments now before us in report stage are an indication of that feeling. It is not too late to do something about it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak this evening in support of my party's position on Bill C-57 and to highlight some of my own personal concerns and some of the concerns of my constituents regarding this bill.
We all recognize that governments need to raise revenue. We know there is no such thing as a free lunch. Ideally, the money we pay as taxes should not be counted as lost but, rather, as a contribution to the common good. But sometimes when we look at government spending habits and its concern with outdated fighter planes and some of its other extravagances, we wonder whether or not this is true. We recognize the importance of our taxes, but we also say that a tax policy should consider many questions in addition to asking how much money can be raised for the government in a specific situation. For example, a tax policy should ask questions concerning the effect of a tax upon the economy in general and upon individual sectors of the economy. It should ask questions about the effect of a given tax upon individuals. Apart from its direct effect upon the economy, it should ask about the effect
of a tax upon the environment, upon the social and cultural fabric of the community and of the nation.
This might be a good place to begin. For example, the act exempts from tax paintings, drawings and pastels, which is good as far as it goes, but it says nothing about original prints. In our society artists do not have a very easy time of it. All but a very few stars have difficulty making a living. However, one area of art which has been growing and provides an important part of many artists' incomes is the sale of limited editions of original prints. Not only does this sale help the artist, but it also helps to democratize art. Art should not be the preserve of a wealthy elite-the Medicis, the Rockefellers and the Thompsons of our world. By exempting paintings and drawings but not original prints, we are discriminating against our ordinary people in favour of the wealthy.
I am particularly concerned about the effect of this discrimination upon many Indian artists. All Canadians can take pride in the recent upsurge of Indian art. I think particularly of Indian artists who use motifs from the west coast of British Columbia and of artists who are painting from their woodland Cree and Ojibway traditions. This art, and the new understanding and respect which it has brought to Indian people, has been largely dependent upon print-making techniques. It is because prints have been available, that artists such as Daphne Odjig, Jackson Beardy, Norville Moriseau and Robert Davidson have become household names in many parts of Canada. Our tax policy should encourage this art and not discourage it. Therefore, I urge the government to accept the amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) and include "original prints" in the list of exemptions.
The government is equally shortsighted in its proposals to tax newspapers which have advertising content beyond a certain percentage. This proposal hits especially hard at small community weeklies. Over the past years, and especially the past year, we have seen the spectacle of large chains taking an ever-greater share of the daily newspaper market in Canada. Corporate takeovers, mergers and shutdown all point to a situation which is very rightly under combines investigation at the present time. As the large dailies move further and further away from local concerns and have less and less contact with local communities, and as they move toward a prepackaged product, the role of community newspapers in our country continues to grow.
For example, in my constituency there is no single daily which serves the entire area, but we are well served by seven community newspapers. These papers are very concerned about the proposed new regulations and the effect that they will have upon their ability to continue publishing. They recognize the government's valid concerns to tax catalogues and sales sheets which have no editorial content at all, but they object to the way in which this concern is being implemented in this bill. For one thing, they point to the manner in which advertising content is defined in the regulations. Instead of
May 28, 1981

counting the amount of paid advertising and then subtracting that from the total space in the newspaper, the regulations begin by narrowly defining editorial content. This way of defining the situation provides a disincentive for charity advertising. It means that little logo fillers for such things as the Participaction program would be counted as advertising. It raises questions about the possibility of newspapers refusing to carry advertisements for certain organizations and using the excuse that carrying the advertisement would bring the newspaper over a certain percentage of advertising content. It raises very serious questions about the whole freedom of the press, which is fundamental to our society. I again urge the government to seriously consider and accept the amendments proposed by my colleague, which would limit the tax to catalogues.
We can look at small businesses and the way in which they are affected by some of the proposals before us, for example, beauty parlours and the tax on cosmetic supplies. Beauty parlours and their operators are truly small businesses and often family enterprises, which have difficulties making ends meet what with maintaining an inventory and adequate equipment. By placing this tax upon supplies which are used in business, it is making it more difficult for these small businesses to continue.
Like other members of my party, I object to the principle of indexed taxation which is being introduced in this bill through the indexation of taxes on alcohol and tobacco. The government already has too much of a stake in inflation. By placing indexation on these taxes we are setting a precedent whereby the government would not have to show any concern at all about bringing in a budget and facing the music in the House of Commons over its taxing policies. Instead, there would simply be automatic tax increases as the cost of living went up, and we have seen no indication from the present government that the cost of living will be going down.
As has been pointed out before, in this bill we have seen the ridiculous bureaucratic definition which exempts some equipment for the handicapped. It exempts braces which are used on the feet and ankles. Surely in this Year of the Disabled the government could recognize that any appliances which are meant to assist disabled people to function better in society should be given tax exempt status. We should not leave these people at the mercy of a stupid bureaucratic decision.
Dynamite is a substance which has been traditionally exempt from taxation. For the first time in our history it is now being taxed. This hits at the construction industry, especially in western Canada. I point out that here we see the government concerned with short-term financial gain-a very small one-but one which has an impact on the environment. For example, we are concerned that industry and buildings should not be built on valuable agricultural land and estuaries, but these are the easiest places to build. In British Columbia, if we are to build away from these areas, blasting is involved and dynamite is required. We are placing a disincentive upon moving away from building on environmentally sensitive areas.
Excise Tax
The New Democratic Party has been urging the government to recognize that small businesses which are involved in collecting sales taxes are subject to a great deal of additional red tape as a result. We urge the government to recognize the contribution these small businesses are making and that it should make provision in this tax bill so that these businesses could withhold 3 per cent of the taxes which they collect, up to a maximum of $1,000. This will not affect large companies such as Eatons and The Bay. However, it will help small businesses. These are the people in our society right now who very desperately need to have some help. At a time when other government policies are discriminating against these people in terms of high interest rates, we should not be passing by an opportunity to make it slightly easier for them to do a job on our behalf which we require them to do.
Again, we can look at the provisions of the bill which exempts equipment specifically designed for use in classrooms. At a time when education is under pressure, another sector of our society which is under considerable pressure today, we should be extending this exemption to include all materials which are used in the classroon, whether or not they had been specifically designed for this.
I would like to draw my remarks to a conclusion by simply pointing out that in its over-all tax policy the government, in the past few years, has been focusing entirely too much upon individuals, small businesses and this sector of society, for tax revenue. It has been ignoring vital areas where profits have been increasing, and taxes have not recognized this. We have heard the news about bank profits being up 58 per cent in the first quarter of this year. We are not doing anything about tapping that source of revenue. Instead, we are continuing to load more and more tax burdens upon individuals and small businesses.
So I urge the government to consider the amendments that the New Democratic Party is putting forward. I urge the government to consider the needs of small businesses, and to consider the social and environmental impacts of some of these taxes, as well as the short-term economic gain which it might make by imposing them.

The number of licences granted from April of last year to April of this year are down. Fifty-nine licenses were granted last year, and this year they are down to 30. 1 do not really know what we must do to make the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources realize what he is doing to our country and to us as Canadians. Honestly, I have never heard such a conglomeration of unadulterated garbage delivered in this House of Commons as I did from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources yesterday. It would imply that he does not know what he is doing. He does not know what he is talking about. We are all going to suffer the consequences if something is not done very shortly.
Evidently, the members of the cabinet are not listening; but I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) sitting in the House tonight. I would hope that he would use his good influence to get through to the cabinet and to try to explain to it exactly what is happening. I would like to tell those who are present in the House tonight that as of May 6 of this year, in the 13-month period, gas prices at the pump have gone up 52 cents. Our policy of 18 cents a gallon tax plus the increases in price, would probably have netted about 37 cents. So Canadians are now paying more because of
the policies of this government and its national energy program. It is disastrous.
I understand that one of the areas which has not been discussed up to the present time is the tax which has been put on Canadians because of the purchase of Petrofina. Does this makes sense to you, Mr. Speaker? It certainly does not to me. I would like to see someone in this House of Commons stand up and try to protect that kind of a policy. Actually, what will happen is that it will undermine the whole industry. How can the government keep on doing that?
It is my understanding that at the present time the federal government has contributed about $1 billion, in one way or another, to Petro-Canada. What return are we as Canadians getting? Are we getting dividends? Are we getting debentures? Are we getting interest? No, we are not getting any of that. It works out to almost $3 billion by the time the whole program is through, if it is not carried on any further. subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITY-INVESTIGATION OF FURTHER SPY RINGS IDENTIFIED BY TASCHEREAU ROYAL COMMISSION
NATIONAL SECURITY-INVESTIGATION OF FURTHER SPY RINGS IDENTIFIED BY TASCHEREAU ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
On April 3 of this year, as reported at page 8946 of Hansard, I obtained from the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) an undertaking to report to me on whether any orders had been issued at any time to bring to a halt inquiries being made into some of the spy rings whose existence was brought to light back in 1945 and 1946 by Igor Gouzenko and made public through the publication of the Taschereau-Kellock report. I am still waiting for that report.
It was not given to me on May 25 when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Kelly) replied to my intervention that evening, as reported at page 9904 of Hansard. Perhaps I will be given the long awaited report in the course of the reply that will be made to my intervention this evening. I hope so, because I raised a cognate question even earlier, on March 30 to be exact, as reported at page 8733 of Hansard.
The Gouzenko report, as the Taschereau-Kellock report is often called, is perhaps not well known by many of the young people today. I would earnestly recommend that it be made compulsory reading for anyone entering university or the public service. It would also be helpful reading for the executives of our large private enterprises and for those who become our trade union leaders. The message it conveys is chilling, but it must not be forgotten. We have allowed ourselves to be lulled to sleep or into a state of complacency on a matter of infiltration and subversion.
There are those, I suspect, in high places today who would prefer that the Gouzenko report be covered with the dust of oblivion. So pertinent is it to today's frightening circumstances that 1 intend to drag it out, dust if off a bit and place on the record in 1981 some of the findings recorded in 1946, some 35
years ago. Let me quote verbatim from page 685 of the report. The first finding reads as follows:
There exists in Canada a fifth column organized and directed by Russian agents in Canada and in Russia.
The second finding reads:
With the fifth column there are several spy rings.
The third finding reads:
We have been able to identify many of the members of one of these rings, namely, that of which Colonel Zabotin was the head in Canada.
These findings lead me directly to the questions to which the Canadian people and I deserve a straightforward answer. First, were any efforts made at the time or later to run down the rings, other than the Zabotin ring, the investigation of which was pursued and people were brought to trial as a result? Second, if such efforts were made, what were the results?
Third, what credence can be placed in reports in the press and elsewhere that those efforts of the RCMP security services to run those other rings to earth were called off by someone in a position of influence. Those rumours persist and it is time they were either put to rest or the truth of them revealed.
In his comments as reported in Hansard on May 25, at page 9904, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Service spoke of four sets of the Taschereau-Kellock documents. He mentioned the location of only three. Therefore, and here is another question I am bound to ask, what of the fourth copy of the transcripts of the Taschereau-Kellock report? Is it complete? How do we know that it is complete? Although the parliamentary secretary was quite categorical in assuring me in that same reply as follows:
-that the exhibits and miscellaneous papers of the Taschereau-Kellock commission involving some 601 original statements, personal notebooks of persons interviewed by the commission, etc., are also stored in the RCMP archives.
Why, I am now bound to ask, are these exhibits and miscellaneous papers not also available to the public under the 30-year rule? Is someone being protected? Is there some reason why they are being maintained beyond the reach of public scholarship or the press, whichever might be the more interesting?
There are more questions here than can be asked in the seven minutes allowed me this evening, and many more than can be answered in the three allowed for the reply. I therefore hope that when the results of the current inquiry into the release of the Gouzenko papers or the Taschereau-Kellock papers are made available to the House, hopefully this month, the minister will make a statement on motions so that some of these questions can be put to him and answers obtained. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITY-INVESTIGATION OF FURTHER SPY RINGS IDENTIFIED BY TASCHEREAU ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer, on behalf of the Solicitor General of Canada, the question put by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) who,
May 28, 1981

really, according to what he says, is feeding the rumour mill. I feel he is doing his best to keep those rumours alive. In recent months, they have certainly been a popular topic in the newspapers.

The hon. member rightly points out that Mr. Gouzenko did in fact state that there were several other spy rings operating in Canada in addition to the one of which he was directly aware. It will be recalled that Mr. Gouzenko disclosed the existence of a spy ring operating on behalf of Soviet military intelligence, the GRU. Mr. Gouzenko claimed that there were other spy rings operating in Canada, some perhaps also under GRU direction, and still others which were under the control of the Soviet state security intelligence organization, the KGB.
This information was also disclosed in the 1946 report of the Taschereau-Kellock commission of inquiry. I might say to the hon. member that an exhibit in any report is part of the report and should be disclosed at the same time. I am just wondering why the hon. member is asking why the exhibits have not been disclosed when the report has not been.
This is not a new question, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, on May 31, 1978, as recorded in Hansard at pages 5920 and 5921, the Solicitor General of the day, the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais), gave a full and complete answer. I reply to a written question by the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt), the minister acknowledged Mr. Gouzenko's claim that there were several espionage rings operating in Canada at the time in question and that it was not true that the RCMP only pursued the investigation of one network. In reply to a request for further details, the solicitor general at the time noted that it was not the policy of the government to comment publicly on individual police and security investigations. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich knows that, and for obvious reasons government policy is not changing.
In the second part of his question the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich makes the allegation that the RCMP investigation into these additional Soviet espionage networks was interrupted or stopped by other members of the public service. This allegation again is almost identical to the assertion referred to in the earlier question by the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville. In his question that hon. member supposed that the government had failed to act in relation to the investigation of these other groups. In fact, the solicitor general at the time advised the House that the government was satisfied that all leads flowing from Mr. Gouzenko's information had been exhaustively pursued and that no further action was required.
I wish to assure my hon. friend that all the information was given at the time and it has not changed since then.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROCEDURE FOR CONVENING FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCES
THE CONSTITUTION-PROCEDURE FOR CONVENING FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 6, 1981, I posed two questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The first one related to the application of clause 35(1)
Adjournment Debate
of the constitutional resolution which will return to this House, and it involved the requirement under that clause for the Prime Minister to call a constitutional conference consisting, in terms of those in attendance, of himself and the provincial premiers. I asked a question as to the usefulness of that particular clause, having regard to the indication of the Prime Minister that day or the day before that he did not intend to attend a meeting called by eight of the ten provincial premiers.
My concern at the time was that it is futile, very clearly, to insert a provision of this nature in the principal and fundamental law of Canada which requires for its application the good will not only of the Prime Minister of the country, but also the good will of ten provincial premiers and, presumably, in the event that the Yukon and Northwest Territories become provinces, ultimately the good will of the premiers of those areas as well. I did not believe it was appropriate that the Prime Minister attend to the request for a meeting, in the fashion he did, without recognizing the harm that he would do to the natural good will which was necessary in order that, first, the provincial premiers attend these intended conferences and, second, something indeed be accomplished thereat.
Fortunately, subsequent to April 6 the Prime Minister did indicate that he would attend such a meeting, and he went on at some length at a later date as well to point out that he hoped the good will that needed to be fostered in Canada would continue after the Supreme Court had ruled. Presumably he meant the Supreme Court would rule in his favour because it was not long after his comments that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), as recently as the latter part of last week, indicated that in the event that the Supreme Court should determine that the autocratic position taken by the federal government is ultra vires, he will see to it that the Supreme Court is used as an instrument to extract from the provinces some of the authorities they are currently exercising.
These matters are significant, and they go to the very roots of the need in our country for government leaders in the provinces and at the federal level to deal with each other on a basis of, if not friendship, at least some form of open congeniality which will produce the well-being desired by the people of Canada. From all indications, what has transpired so far is a clear demonstration for all who have witnessed the proceedings, that this government is hardly the government to be involved in the process of establishing such a fundamental change in the nature of our country.
My supplementary question dealt with the acknowledged legal concept that in the event the charter of rights is established as contemplated by this resolution, the Supreme Court of Canada will in fact, as is the case in other jurisdictions, legislate through its interpretive judgments dealing with what the words in this charter mean. That is a simple principle of law and one which surely must be recognized by the Prime Minister who, I understand, was called to the bar, although I doubt he has ever practised. At least I do not think he has ever practised.
Instead of dealing with the issue which was raised in the question, the Prime Minister dealt with the myth that for 54

May 28, 1981
Adjournment Debate
years we have been trying to obtain a consensus. Nothing is further from the truth. The alleged charter of rights and freedoms with which we are presently concerned and which gives rise to most of the dispute throughout our nation was first presented to the people of Canada, to this Parliament and to the provincial premiers in October of 1980. October of 1980 is the fall of last year, and 54 years never enters into a determination of the time within which we have been concerned about this issue.
Then the Prime Minister went on in answer to my substantive question to say the following:
As to the question itself regarding the role of the courts and Parliament, it seems to me that the hon. member is under a misapprehension. What I have said is that both branches of government should be autonomous and should operate autonomously. It is our job to legislate. It is the court's job to judge whether the legislation is intra vires or ultra vires.
That is not the question I was asking, Mr. Speaker. I know it is the court's job to determine whether legislation is intra vires or ultra vires, but that was not the question. The question was very simple: does the court not in fact legislate, having determined that it is intra vires, and thereby preclude this Parliament and all subsequent parliaments from ever determining whether they may change the words in the charter. That was the question.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a prime minister who responds in the fashion this one has does no service to the public or this Elouse. Very clearly this Parliament is the supreme parliament of all parliaments because it has fixed the basic law of the country, if this package goes through, and no subsequent parliament under any circumstances will be able to change the law as this Parliament has enacted it. Now that is the death blow to the democratic process, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROCEDURE FOR CONVENING FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have three comments in relation to what the hon. member has said. First, we have not been discussing a charter of rights just since 1980. A charter of rights has been discussed for at least the last 12 years. There have been three distinct studies, and I advise my learned friend to read them. The first was the Canadian Bar Association, the second was the Pepin-Robarts report and the third was the parliamentary committee, all dealing with the charter of rights.
We have been talking about this for 54 years, Mr. Speaker, and once again at the tail end of this debate we are going back to process and procedure and I say that at some point my good friend, the hon. member for North York (Mr. Gamble) will have to say yes or no, I stand for a charter; yes or no, I stand for aboriginal rights; yes or no, I stand for mobility rights; yes or no, I stand for rights for the handicapped; yes or no, I stand for non-discrimination of women and the aged. I think the time has come when the people of this country are saying to the opposition that you can no longer hide behind the premiers, you have to come out and say whether a law in Newfoundland that disallows unions is to be tolerated any
longer; whether a law in Quebec which discriminates, prejudices and padlocks Jehovah witnesses is to be tolerated any longer.
Now either you stand for these things or you do not. We all represent the people; the premiers, the members of this honourable assembly, members of councils of municipalities. And at some point you have to make the decision on what is right and wrong and what is hiding behind procedure.
What did the premiers come up with? The Hon. Sterling Lyon is still against the charter. I heard nothing about minority language rights coming from the Hon. Rene Levesque. I heard nothing from the Hon. Brian Peckford. I heard nothing except another checkerboard suggestion, the fifth one that has come from either the premiers or the opposition, that would allow the right to a jury in one province and not in another, rights of the aboriginals in one province and none in the other provinces because, and you know I am telling the truth, the checkerboard formula provides that if it affects the provinces, as these things do, they can opt out. There can only be one right of mobility, that is the right of a Canadian to move across this country and work where he wishes. I say that to meet with the premiers at this late date to discuss what they are proposing would be a disservice to this country and the people we represent.

(A)	PREPARATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SUMMIT MEETING
(B)	IMPLEMENTATION OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS
(C)	QUERY RESPECTING CANADIAN SUPPORT FOR UNITED STATES POLICIES

Mr. Speaker, my question is in relation to a question I asked the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on May 20 in regard to the policy recommendations Canada will put to the summit meeting this summer. I asked very specifically if Canada was going to have a policy uniquely different from that of the United States, a made-in-Canada policy as it relates to the entire question of North-South. At that time the Right Hon. Prime Minister replied to me:
We know from the statements made by the U.S. administration that they are more keen on bilateral aid and perhaps aid from the private sector than on multilateral and public aid. This is not the point of view of Canada or of other summit countries.
To my mind what the Prime Minister has told me is that Canada is not going to follow the policy of the United States which at this time is going to be linked more closely to bilateral aid. This basically means that the United States will give aid to another country but will be very much directing it.
The reason I asked to have my question reviewed tonight was that prior to it, at a meeting of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on April 21, 1981, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) said exactly the opposite. The Prime Minister seemed to say
May 28, 1981

that Canada would move away from bilateral aid to multilateral aid, meaning that Canada will join with other countries and have an aid program with a much broader spectrum than this direct deal. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said the following:
-so we are certainly moving, at the present time, more in the direction of expanding bilateral aid than of expanding multilateral aid.
There seems to be no clear policy about how Canada's program of aid will function. I appreciate very much the difficulty of truly aiding somebody else. Perhaps one of the most difficult verbs in the English language is the verb to aid. How do we help someone else? How do we help someone else so that the other person is helped and does not become, in a sense, subservient?
Last summer we in the North-South committee visited the United Nations during its special session. At that time we had an opportunity to speak with Donald McHenry, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. In his discussions with us, he summarized, perhaps, better than anyone else I have ever heard, the notion of aid. He simply said that aid is for aid. Aid is not to fight communism. Aid is not to build up the industrial sector. Aid is not to buy off somebody. Aid is to aid.
We will be hosting the summit meeting in Ottawa and later we will be one of the two nations taking part in the other summit meetings in Mexico and Australia. England and Canada will be the only two countries sharing the entire summit meetings. At this time in Canadian history, I think it is extremely important for the House of Commons and the people of Canada to know exactly what the policy of this government is in relation to the question of what is aid and why we are aiding.
I have heard the recent reports of the business group which deals with Latin America. This group is very happy with Canada's aid program because it means more business for them; it is a kind of subsidized business grant. As I question what is our policy on aid, I would like to read into the record what Mr. Masse, the president of CIDA, who is responsible for the Canadian aid program, said in an interview which appeared in The Financial Post on May 16. He said:
Investment in big projects is all very well, but it's not really efficient unless you also change the way people use capital ... So now we intend to invest more in people, particularly in the areas of occupational training, management skills, health and education. It's a way of increasing the productivity of people themselves.
I gather what Mr. Masse says now is that he is looking upon aid as something which is being sent and that he is trusting other people at a very low level, not big projects which will benefit Canadian industry, but people there who need the aid. They will make the decision as to how it will be used. I would like to ask the government what Canada's basic principles and philosophies about aid are and who is making the policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
Adjournment Debate
would like to assure the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) that his concerns are being considered by the Government of Canada.
Preparations for the July summit are progressing well. The personal representatives of the heads of state and government will be meeting shortly in Vancouver. It is still difficult to say with certainty what topics will be given priority at the summit. Some heads of state have been elected only recently, among them Mr. Mitterrand, and they will have to have the opportunity to express their opinions as partners about the various themes to be considered at the summit. For the moment, we presume that the summit will deal with the five traditional economic subjects: macroeconomics, monetary and financial matters, trade, energy and, naturally, North-South relations.
On the last subject, the report on "Aid Policies and Procedures and Other Contributions to Developing Countries", requested by the heads of state in Venice, will no doubt give rise to in-depth discussion.
The government has been very pleased with the contributions which the parliamentary task force has made to North-South issues both in terms of its recommendations about appropriate Canadian policies and of the all-party stimulus it has provided for public discussion of these important issues within Canada. The government's initial attitude to the basic thrust of the task force report is very positive. Its individual recommendations have been the subject of close study over recent months and are currently under consideration by ministers, and detailed responses are expected shortly.
Obviously, Canada's North-South policy does not parallel that of the United States which may choose to give priority to bilateral assistance and to the private sector in order to meet the needs of the developing world. We do trust however that they will not neglect the multilateral dimension of aid and we hope that the summit will examine certain key areas of relations with developing countries where concrete progress would be possible. We are thinking particularly of the needs of the Third World with respect to energy and the development of agricultural production and food. There is substantial agreement among the summit countries on the objectives to be promoted, but there are differences of opinion on the means of achieving those objectives. It is our hope that the summit discussions will help to reconcile the different points of view, and it is from this standpoint that we will approach the North-South issues with the United States and other summit countries at the Ottawa Summit.
